On Monday

He gave a definite answer with regard to the article itself but did not answer at the time, and] I imagine was not in a position to. do so, the specific question I asked, which was:
Was the recent visit of Sir Maurice Hankey to Canada made the occasion of a discussion or consideration of any plan of empire defence by any member of the government, or by any official or officials of the government, acting under the authority of any minister of the crown ?
The Prime Minister said that he would examine the situation in detail to see whether any further reply should be made than that which he gave. May I say to him that I shall be glad to put the inquiry in the form of a question on the order paper if he prefers to have further time for consideration before giving an answer. If, however, he is prepared to give a definite reply with respect to my question, and the implications conveyed by the article to which I referred that would be more satisfactory.

As I indicated, I had no notice
of the question, but I felt that it was one that should be answered immediately in order that no wrong impressions might be given to the people of Canada. The answer to the question as put is, no. I know of no conversations with respect to empire defence,
Empire Defence Plan

in the sense in which I assume that term is used, which were carried on by Sir Maurice Hankey with any officer or officers of any of the departments, with the authority of the government, or with anyone else, so far as I know, except, as I found on inquiry, that Sir Maurice Hankey did see the chief of the general staff, saw the camps at Roekcliffe, and matters of that sort. I think he called on the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs and sat with him for an hour, and I believe he accepted the hospitality of the right hon. gentleman opposite. He had many conversations with friends whom he had met in previous years, and I had a few words of conversation with him-not an extensive conversation-and certainly there was no discussion of empire defence in any sense, as far as I know. Nor was any such discussion authorized by the government on the part of any official or officials of the departments in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking part in this debate, but there are one or two points on which I should like to make a few remarks, so I shall take this opportunity of doing so. I notice that the following words have been put in the mouth of His Excellency, in the speech from the throne:
In the anxious years through which you have passed, you have been the witnesses of grave defects and abuses in the capitalist system.
Certainly this is a great admission and one which we are very glad to see, because we have claimed that the system has been defective for a great many years. Further on in the speech from the throne 1 find these words:
These require modifications in the capitalist system to enable that system more effectively to serve the people.
I was delighted, in reading one of the Prime Minister's radio speeches, to find that he made the statement that the system was made for man, not man for the system. Up to the present time-and this has been very true, as the last speaker stated-the people have suffered a great deal at the hands of the system because a real effort was being made to make that system work even though it might be at the expense of the public. Therefore it is a great step in the right direction, it seems to me, to have the Prime Minister of this country publicly admit, both outside and inside this house, that the system under which we are working is not satisfactory, and that it must be altered in the interests of the public at large.
In the speech from the throne reference was made to the Natural Products Marketing Act. I am not going to deal with that measure beyond saying a few words, because that matter was thoroughly dealt with a short time ago by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman). I do want to say, however, that I think this is one of the most constructive acts ever brought before this house, and I believe that the more it is understood in the country, and the more we are able to make proper use of it, the more we will realize the value of that legislation, and the more we will come to believe that

The Address-Mr. Spencer
when it was passed a year ago a very great step was taken in the right direction.
Reference was also made to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and I rose particularly to say a few words with regard to that legislation. I think that measure, which was designed to enable the farmers in particular to get out from underneath a certain amount of their load of debt, because of the impossibility of the farming population carrying on under the load they are now attempting to carry, was very badly needed. The machinery set up makes it possible for the debtors and creditors to come together to find ways and means of reducing the total amount of the debt owing. It was surmised and hoped that the creditors would meet the debtors and reduce the sum total of debts to a figure which would enable the farmer to carry on his wrork and retain his home. When the debts were cut down to that figure it was presumed that the farmer then would be on a sound financial footing and would be able to get financed by the farm loan board so that he could pay off his creditors.
If the act had worked out in that way I think we would have done a very fine piece of work, but we find that in some provinces -I do not say all-the farm loan boards do not see their way clear to advance the money to the debtors which would enable them to pay off their creditors. In those circumstances it does not matter in what position the debtor farmer is left, at the will of the creditors, if the farm loan board refuses to allow him to make use of its facilities. In such cases this measure will not be the success we hoped. In certain provinces we find that those in charge of the administration of the farm loan boards have taken the very definite stand that they are not going to be very enthusiastic in trying to make that act work in order to meet the needs of the debtors, even after the debts have been cut down considerably. In that case it means that the debts have not been cut down sufficiently. If the farm loan boards cooperate there are great possibilities in this legislation, and with the power given the Minister of Finance a year ago to buy upwards of $40,000,000 of farm loan bonds, a very serious situation with regard to agriculture can be readily met.
The speech from the throne further goes on to speak of the Bank of Canada as an instrument of national policy to direct the better utilization of the credit resources of Canada. I do hope that this is not what we might term lip service, because here there is a chance to make the greatest possible use of our national credit. I hope there will be no hesi-92582-10
tation in doing so. In the speech from the throne we find advocated many measures in the way of reform. There is no doubt that if these reforms are brought about they will entail considerable expenditure. I do hope that the necessary money will not be collected from taxation, except to the extent that the very large incomes may be more heavily taxed; I hope the fullest use may be made of the national credit in order that these reforms may be carried out.
It is suggested that better provision should be made to protect the worker from unemployment, and in sickness and old age. This has been advocated from this corner of the house for a number of years, and I am delighted to see it in the speech from the throne. It has occurred to me, as it must have occurred to all hon. members of this house in the last few years, that it has been strange to find so many old men still hanging on to their jobs, perhaps because they are not seventy years of age or because they have not been in the country long enough to become entitled to the very small old age pension we now give our old people. In those circumstances they have refused to give up their jobs, because they would be put on the dole. As a result we find our younger population out of work in very large numbers, and we have had to open camps all across Canada to take care of these able, virile and in some cases well educated young men. It does seem to me that we are doing something entirely wrong in keeping the old men at work while we put these young, healthy men into camps. If this statement in the speech from the throne means anything I certainly hope it means that we are going to alter that state of affairs in order to give men, say over sixty, an opportunity to take things a little easier through an old age pension, and at the same time give the young men of the country an opportunity to find work.
According to the speech from the throne a survey is to be made of the national debt structure. I am very glad to see this statement. The house will remember that last year we in this part of the house introduced a resolution along this very line. So we are glad to find this statement in the speech from the throne, for it makes us believe that something is really going to be done in this respect.
I notice in the speech from the throne that there will be an extension of the facilities for long term and intermediate credits. I sincerely hope something will be done to make the farm loan board more operative and give

The Address-Mr. Spencer

better service than it is giving at the present time. The reference to minimum wages and a maximum working week is I believe a step in the right direction. Hon. members to my right will correct me if I am wrong when I state that that was one plank in the Liberal platform of 1919. I had the privilege of sitting in this house for nine years when that party happened to be in power, yet we do not find any mention of this legislation until the year 1935. I trust nothing will hinder the passage of any legislation along these lines.
A further statement in the speech from the throne refers to necessary alterations in the incidence of taxation so that it will more directly conform to capacity to pay. That is a move in the right direction. I am reminded of the budgets brought to this house in the years 1927 and 1928 when we found that the government of that day decided to decrease the income tax on large incomes a procedure which I have always thought was a distinct mistake. In good times, when money is plentiful and business is brisk we should keep up our taxation so that we may put something by for a rainy day, that is create a sinking fund. It is much easier to collect extra money in good times than to collect it 'when times are bad and cash is scarce.
Turning again to the speech from the throne I find there are to be safeguards for the consumer and primary producer against unfair trading practices. When he grows stock or grain the farmer finds himself in the position of a producer. We know only too well about the miserably low prices he has had to accept for his farm produce in the past few years. On the other hand we find he is in the position of a consumer when he must buy his repairs, machinery or binder twine. He is a consumer when he has to buy food, and particularly that food which although originally from the farm has been processed in a factory and is returned to him at a very greatly enhanced price. I am quite certain those people living on the farms will view with a great deal of interest this particular clause in the speech from the throne because they stand to benefit not only as producers but as consumers, if the legislation introduced reflects the spirit we hope will be manifested.
We find in the speech from the throne that we will be invited to enact measures to regulate, in the public interest, concentrations in production and distribution. No doubt some legislation of that sort will be introduced when we receive the report from the price spreads commission. At the present moment rMr. Spencer.]
I am not going to make special reference to that commission because I hope we shall have plenty of opportunity at a later time to discuss the work it has been doing and the findings it has made.
We find further we will be invited to enact measures to provide the investing public with means to protect itself against exploitation. This I believe has particular reference to watered stock. I shall simply remind the house that not only during the life of the last government but in the early years this government held office the matter of watered stock was discussed by hon. members sitting in this corner of the house with the object of reform but nothing was done at either time. Although such action is late I am pleased the government has placed in the speech of His Excellency a statement intimating that they are going to attempt to solve the problem.
Turning again to the speech from the throne we find there will be introduced a reform in our penitentiaries system, and that consideration is being given to the Borstal system. I have no doubt the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and other hon. members who for many years past have recommended reforms in our penitentiaries will appreciate this clause, despite the fact reforms are overdue. We shall watch with a great deal of interest the legislation which will be introduced by the government, and will be pleased to learn how far they intend to go in their reform program.
It gives me pleasure to note that there is to be a reorganization in the government service. Whether or not we happen to agree with many of the Prime Minister's policies we have to give him credit for making very necessary and worth while changes in the Department of Finance during the time he was minister of that department. I am quite sure no one could be better qualified to take the initiative in a reorganization of our whole civil service than is the present Prime Minister of Canada. I note further in the speech from the throne that an economic council will be set up to advise the ministers upon all economic questions concerning our national welfare. Here again I am pleased to welcome the suggestion, one which has been made at least twice from this corner of the house. Upon each occasion it was recommended on our behalf by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman).
Hon. members in this part of the chamber are not greatly interested in what political party places legislation on the statute books; we are far more interested in seeing legis-

The Address-Mr. Heaps
lation placed there. If the present government is prepared to place upon our statute books the legislation mentioned in the speech from the throne I am quite sure it will receive the fullest support from hon. members in this corner of the house on any legislation we have suggested in the past. People have been looking for some action, and I am not going to blame the Prime Minister if some think he has made a volte face. If he is doing something worth while or constructive he should not be criticized. Very often a change is a sign of progress. I agrei with the hon. member who preceded me that many of the suggestions are salve; I am ready to admit that. At the same time it is better that a doctor should recognize the sickness of his patients and be prepared to administer a salve and follow with a real remedy than not to recognize the sickness at all. The present government apparently recognizes that the nation is sick and it is prepared to take some action. If in the nine years it held office the late government had had the courage to come forward with these reforms I would have paid it the same compliment and would have given it the same hearty support as I shall give the present government on the reforms suggested in the speech from the throne.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a few observations I wish to make at this time. I wish particularly to address myself to certain questions that were raised by the Prime Minister in his radio addresses and in the speech from the throne to which I have given a good deal of attention during the years I have been a member of this house.
The present session reminds me somewhat of the session of 1926. I think those hon. members who were members of the house at that time will bear in mind the legislation that was passed during that memorable session, and one of the pieces of legislation which made such a lasting impression on the country was the old age pension act. We got the old age pension act through parliament during that session and it became the law a year or so subsequent. To-day there must be approximately 40,000 people throughout the Dominion of Canada who are receiving the benefits of that legislation. I said that there was some similarity between that session and this session of 1935. In 1926 the government was not a very stable government; they had a very small majority in this house, and it appears now that the present government is not very stable. It appears further that about the only time that we can expect to have enacted social legislation 92582-1(U
that is worth while is when we have not a stable government in power; and there, Mr. Speaker, is the similarity between the two sessions.
Now on the eve of an election we are to be favoured, and I am very pleased to see it, with some social legislation which I hope will confer equal benefits and advantages upon the people of Canada as did the old age pension act of 1926.
It has been suggested by the Prime Minister and those associated with him that there is going to be a series of drastic reforms in the economic structure of this dominion. The fact that these proposals have been made, that these reforms have been suggested to parliament and the country, is in the first place, in my humble opinion, a clear admission that the policies pursued by the government for the past four years have been a failure so far as relieving the economic conditions that have prevailed in this dominion. It is an admission that high tariffs have not proven a remedy for the evils from which we are suffering, that the dumping laws have been no remedy, that the public works that have been inaugurated to relieve unemployment and the dole which has been given to millions of our people have not proven a remedy for the economic ills of this dominion.
But there is this one thing at least that I am thankful for to the Prime Minister, and that is that he has brought a reality into the situation that was formerly lacking in all the public discussions throughout Canada. Now it appears that the problem of employment and the problem of unemployment are about to become the paramount issues. I am very glad that such is the case, for during the past nine or ten years that I have been a member of this house, year in and year out I have brought to the attention of parliament proposals in the nature of reforms and various suggestions that have been made by the small group of which I happen to be a member and which received at that time only scant consideration. If time will permit I hope to put on the records of this house some of those proposals.
The government's new proposals include unemployment insurance, insurance against sickness and invalidity, and insurance against old age. They promise to bring in legislation to regulate the hours of labour and also wages. There are also to be a number of relief works instituted in various parts of the dominion. But at the very best, Mr. Speaker, relief works and the dole are only temporary in their character, and if we are to deal fund-
The Address-Mr. Heaps

amentally with this problem of unemployment we have to go far beyond merely providing relief works for those who happen to be out of work.
The other day the Prime Minister made reference to a loan of 5100,000,000 which he had obtained in the United States in the year 1930 for the purpose of giving relief to the unemployed of this country, and for the purpose of carrying on public relief projects. I had no objection at that time, in the short session of 1930, to the Prime Minister going to New York, and if I remember correctly to the firm of Morgan and Company and obtaining this loan for the dominion, but it did *seem to me an anomalous procedure, and I -would not have referred to it to-day except that the Prime Minister brought it to the attention of the house in his speech during this debate.
That money was required to give to the men and women who were out of work in this country sustenance and relief. A portion of that money was earmarked for what has been termed the dole, to provide food, clothing and shelter to the men, women and children of Canada who at that time most unfortunately were without these necessities. It seemed so ridiculous to me because we had food, clothing and shelter in this country in abundance. Out on the prairies we had more wheat and more food than we knew what to do with. Our warehouses were full of clothing, and our carpenters and builders were walking the streets anxious to construct homes for the people to live in, and yet Mr. Speaker, before our people, before the great masses who were out of work and hungry in this country could eat the foodstuffs which they themselves had produced, they had to get permission from Morgan and Company in the city of New York. If you can show me a more anomalous and ridiculous situation than for us to have to go to a foreign country to get permission to eat the foodstuffs which we ourselves have produced, and are not allowed to consume I would like to know where you could possibly find it.
It has become quite a common and almost a fashionable thing during the past few months to condemn the capitalist system. This afternoon I am not going to condemn capitalists. I have condemned the system quite long enough now. The Prime Minister in his addresses has spoken on more than one occasion of the defects of the capitalist system, and I have been very anxious to hear him speak more particularly on what in his opinion were the defects in the system and what exactly would be done to relieve the

situation. I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that we can get rid of unemployment and the evils of unemployment within the confines of the capitalist structure.
May I here refer for a few moments to what they have 'been doing in the United States during the last couple of years. There they had a vast army of unemployed, the same as we have had here, and for a period of two years they have been- pumping into the economic structure of that country approximately thirty billions of dollars-a staggering sum of money which the average human mind can hardly realize. And yet in spite of the fact that they have pumped into the economic life of that country thirty billions of dollars, conditions in the United States are hardly any better to-day than they were two or three years ago. There must be a reason for that. If the pumping of so much money into their economic structure can have so little effect, then naturally one is impelled to ask:	Why is it that in spite of all these
efforts that have been made in the United States there still persists this unemployment problem which as yet they have hardly touched? Here may I say that in discussing this question in this house a year or so agio I made observations to this effect: I said that what they are trying to do in the United States is to create a cooperative structure within the confines of the competitive capitalist structure, and I said that it was impossible to have a structure which was at one and the same time both competitive and cooperative. I claimed that sooner or later one must give way to the other, and much sooner than one might have expected the cooperative efforts of the government of the United States have given way to the competitive system, and probably within a comparatively short time we shall find the United States proceeding on completely different lines in a further attempt to solve the unemployment conditions that prevail to the south of the line. Therefore, if there has been no basic improvement in conditions to the south of the line as a result of the spending of the vast sums of money to which I have referred, it means that if we in this country are to end or even to alleviate unemployment we shall have to look in some other direction than that which has been followed in the United States. At all times we have looked in the direction of creating more work to provide more employment. I submit that our first and basic consideration should be to provide not more work but more consumption of goods among the people of Canada. There is to-day no lack of productive capacity if the

The Address-Mr. Heaps
people were given an opportunity to consume; but there is that great lack of consumptive opportunity amongst the great masses of our people. We have found during the past few years that there has been a wide spread between actual production and actual consumption, and unless we can get a reasonable balance between consumption and production then we shall continue to have unemployment and poverty on our hands and in our midst just as we have at the present time.
As a member of the labour group in this house, I say that we are strongly opposed, bitterly opposed, to the curtailment of production. And we have opposed it from the very first. I well remember that when the Minister of Finance was over in Europe a year or two ago he spoke about the people there consuming more of our wheat, and this expression I lauded. But why reserve that increased consumption for the people of Europe? What about our own people in Canada? Have they no prior consideration to our own production in the dominion? Why should they not be entitled to consume more than they have the opportunity of doing at present? I submit that our whole effort should be to increase the consumptive opportunities of the people of Canada; or, to put it another way, there must be a more equitable distribution of the wealth produced in Canada than there has been up to the present time.
The plans, either of this or of any future government, if the economic situation is to be relieved, should be considered from this particular angle, because I hold that it is only as we increase the actual consumption of goods by the people of the country that we shall make any impression upon the economic distress now prevalent. Unemployment is inherent in the capitalistic system. I want to see unemployment and all that it implies in the way of poverty and so forth entirely eliminated. But if we cannot have it eliminated immediately I am prepared to do all I can as a member of this house to alleviate and mitigate conditions with the ultimate objective of completely eliminating unemployment from our midst.
Now what the average citizen of Canada is looking for is some security in life. This he has not at the present time. The million or so -who to-day are on relief have no security and very little hope for the future. The other day the Prime Minister gave the house some figures in reference to the unemployment situation. He claimed that between 1932 and the present time, from a peak of 750,000 those out of work had decreased to
approximately 400,000; I do not know very much about these figures and I have not had time to examine them, but I presume they have been prepared by competent statisticians. I do know however that in the large industrial centres where unemployment is prevalent, where there are so many people on relief and where the relief figures bear eloquent testimony to the unemployment situation as it exists in most of those large centres, the decrease in the number on relief is approximately 10 per cent. If this is the case there must certainly be a most serious problem confronting us at the present time.
When I look at the government's proposals I want to see how they fit in with some of the suggestions I have made. How would they give the average Canadian more security in life than he has to-day? How would they give him a better standard of living than he now enjoys? How would they give the man or woman out of work an opportunity to obtain a livelihood and work?
Coming to unemployment insurance, I may point out that this is a matter to which I have directed the attention of the houses for the past nine years as the records of Hansard will show. To my way of thinking, unemployment insurance is a very desirable objective. It is a proposal which I will support provided the bill meets the essentials of what I should regard as a comprehensive scheme of unemployment insurance in this dominion. But to-day we have reached a stage in the economic life of this country where any scheme of unemployment insurance if it is on a contributory basis will take care, not of those who are out of work at the present time-they will be left alone-but of those who are to-day employed and who may a year or two hence find themselves out of work. If therefore we deal with the unemployment insurance problem any measure such as that is not going to alleviate the immediate distress among our Canadian citizens who are at present out of work.
With regard to sickness and invalidity, any bill which is brought in and which will ensure against these evils will without the slightest doubt receive my unhesitating support. But there is a question which I must ask with regard to old age pensions. It has been foreshadowed by the Prime Minister in somewhat ambiguous terms that he is going to bring into being a system of contributory old age pensions. I say his language is rather ambiguous because I hardly understand what he means when he .speaks of a contributory system of old age pensions. If he implies that he is going to place on a contributory basis
i50
The Address-Mr. Heaps

the pension system which is now in effect in Canada, then I will strongly oppose any bill of that kind. Any pension which is received under the provisions of the act of 1926 is given as a right: in fact, in my opinion, it is more of a right than the pensions given generals, judges and officials of the government. But if the Prime Minister's statement implies that he is going to follow in effect the system in Great Britain, then I am prepared to give it the sympathetic consideration which such a proposal naturally deserves. For in Great Britain there is a dual system of old age pensions. Between the ages of 65 and 70 it is on a contributory basis; after 70 the entire cost of the pension becomes a responsibility of the government. If there is going to be a contributory old age pension in Canada, I do hope the first thing the Prime Minister will do will be to bring down the age level of those who are entitled to its Benefits and thereby perhaps help somewhat to relieve a congested labour market.
I now come to minimum wage laws and a maximum work week. I attach more importance to a minimum wage law and a maximum work week than I do to the proposed measure dealing with unemployment insurance. I attach far more importance to that aspect of his proposed legislation than I do to anything else appearing in the speech from the throne, for if the Prime Minister or the government wills and parliament wills, by establishing a low maximum working week and a high minimum wage, he can do more to relieve the unemployment situation than anything else he has done during the whole time he has been in office. The time has come when there should be a complete revision of our maximum working week and minimum wage laws. Our minimum wage laws are altogether too low and our working week is altogether too high. If we are ever going to absorb the masses of our unemployed into the productive life of this country, this can be done only by a restriction of the hours of labour. I know there are many hon. members, possibly on both sides of the house, who have a strong objection to both minimum wage laws and a maximum work week. Well, those laws have been in effect in this country for quite a number of years, but I believe by attempting to put a national law into effect, one that will be the same in all the provinces as regards both wages and a maximum work week, we can go a long way towards doing something for those who at the present time are unemployed. I know it will be said that this will have the effect of increasing price levels. I know it will also be said that it is

pretty hard to do all these things within the confines of the existing economic structure. I realize such a law, that is for a maximum work week and a minimum wage, may have the effect of cutting very deeply into the profits of many of our corporations, but if I have to choose between the profits of our corporations and providing for the well-being of the masses of our people, I am going to be on the side of the masses. As I said before, the spread between wages, which in many ways means consumption, and production must be reduced, and one of the few ways by which we can reduce that spread is by insisting on and maintaining a high minimum wage level in our industrial life.
I come now to another point in the discussion concerning the problems with which I have just dealt: I come to the question of the attitude of the provinces. I know some of our provinces are very jealous of their rights. I am not going to blame any of them for that jealousy, but I think there comes a time in (the life of possibly all of us when something of great importance must transcend our own personal interest. So now in the life of the Dominion of Canada there has come a time when the enactment of legislation as foreshadowed by the government must take precedence over certain of the rights of the provinces. It has been realized time and time again that as regards the questions of minimum wage laws, maximum working week, unemployment insurance and so on, there must be in the dominion a centralized authority, because without such an authority we could have no successful scheme in operation of any of these laws. Instead of there being opposition from the provinces at this juncture, I hope every one of the nine provinces will attempt to cooperate with parliament and the government, however one cares to put it, so that there may be brought into effect in the dominion something that will be of lasting benefit to our people. The common weal of the Canadian people at this time transcends in importance some of the constitutional issues that may be raised by those who are not in favour of this form of legislation and who no doubt will be opposed to it. No province can isolate itself from the rest of the dominion any more than the dominion can isolate itself from the other nations of the world. So I sincerely hope the provinces will join the central authority, namely, the federal parliament, in its corporate capacity to bring about legislation that will at least leave, as I said before, a lasting impression on the social [DOT]and economic life of the dominion.

The Address-Mr. Heaps
I said previously a word or two in regard to the efforts that have been made by hon. members in this -corner of the house to further social legislation. I am glad to see that after all these thirteen years of effort by various members of the independent groups we have at last reached a stage where the feeling is practically unanimous that legislation along the lines we have suggested should be put upon -the statute books. I hope when the legislation comes before the house none of us will be disappointed. I accept the assurances of the government that the legislation will be of such a character that it will accomplish something worth while.
May I now go back to give a brief synopsis of the situation. In 1919, after the war, when there was a great deal of unrest in the dominion, the then -government appointed a commission to inquire into industrial unrest and it was asked to make as speedy a report as possible on many of the problems of that day. That commission reported that among other matters, industrial unrest was caused by unemployment -a-nd the fear of unemployment. In other words, they felt that unemployment and the fear of unemployment caused amongst the workers a sense of insecurity and this was more the cause of unreat than anything else they were able to ascertain during the period of investigation. So they recommended another committee to investigate the whole question of unemployment, sickness and invalidity insurance with a view to early legislation and with, of course the federal government acting in the matter.
A few months later at a convention of the Liberal party, they embodied the proposals of this royal commission in one of the planks of their platform. If I may read the exact plank of the platform of the party, it is as follows:
That in so far as may be practicable having regard for Canada's financial position an adequate system of insurance against unemployment, sickness, dependence in old age and other disabilities which will include old age pensions and maternity benefits should be instituted by the federal government, in conjunction with the governments of the several provinces, and that on matters pertaining to industrial and social legislation an effort should be made to overcome any question of jurisdiction between the dominion and provinces by effective cooperation between the several provinces.
Now let me turn from this plank in the Liberal platform of 1919 and jump to the Conservative platform of 1927, adopted at the convention held in Winnipeg in the fall of that year. The following resolution under the heading Capital and Labour was adopted and inserted in its platform:
So far as is practicable to support social legislation to design and conserve human life, health and temperance, to relieve distress during periods of unemployment, sickness and old age.
It will be observed that there is a good deal in common between what the Conservative party proposed in 1927 and what the Liberal party proposed in 1919.
Then I come to the parliamentary session of 1926. There we find in the records of the house some of the earliest efforts made to get social legislation enacted by parliament. On January 7, 1926, my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) wrote certain communications to the then leader of the house, now the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and to the then leader of the opposition now the leader of the government in the Senate Mr. Meighen. These communications have been put on the records of the house so often that I shall not weary the house with them at the present time, and will just say that we received communications in reply from both the leaders. From the then leader of t-he opposition, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, we received replies most evasive and unsatisfactory in regard to unemployment insurance and old age pensions, but we received from the then Prime Minister, now the leader of the opposition, a reply more definite and satisfactory; and as a result no doubt of our efforts during that period we had legislation introduced in 1926 which subsequently became law. I am informed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) that the number of old age pensioners in Canada to-day is approximately 87,000. I had put the figure at 40,000. I am glad of the correction; it goes to show how beneficial that legislation was and how worthwhile were the efforts of my hon. colleague for Winnipeg North Centre and myself.

speechtext:
I am speaking of the federal government. I know that British Columbia is a remarkable province, has a remarkable contingent in this house and some remarkable legislation.
On Wednesday, March 16, 1927, the following resolution was introduced in the house by myself:
That, in the opinion of this house, the committee on industrial and international relations be instructed to investigate and report on the establishment of a system of insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity.
This motion was talked out on that occasion, on a Wednesday afternoon, which I remember very well and about which the less I say the better.
In the following year, on February 16, 1928,
I again introduced the same resolution word for word, but the government of the day, now the opposition, accepted the motion and it was referred to the committee on industrial and international relations. For the rest

of the session of 1928 and the session of 1929 the matter was under review by that committee. However, before it went back to the committee, on February 14, 1929, I asked that the same resolution as I moved the year before be adopted by the house in order to give the committee the opportunity of considering it during the session of 1929.
In both years the committee made a report to this house. That report was in many respects somewhat ambiguous. They favoured the principle, but I have long since come to the conclusion that a little bit of action is worth more than many resolutions in the House of Commons.
On June 1, 1928, the committee submitted to this house its first report, recognizing the necessity of providing some form of unemployment insurance, and that it would have to be dealt with before very long. It also recognized the question of jurisdiction as between the provinces and the dominion in clause 3 of the report. I think we all recognize that there is this question of jurisdiction as between federal and provincial authorities, a very important issue.
On May 1, 1929, when the second report came before this house, I was not satisfied that the committee had gone as far as it could. It is not enough merely to point out the difficulties inherent in our constitution in connection with this sort of legislation. On Thursday, May 23, the chairman of the committee submitted the report in the house for its approval, and I asked by way of amendment that the report be referred back to the committee on industrial and international relations with the following instruction:
That the said report of the select standing committee on industrial and international relations be not now concurred in but that it be referred back to the select standing committee on industrial and international relations with instructions that they have power to amend the same by adding thereto a clause recommending that all the provinces of the dominion be requested to pass legislation under which the jurisdiction in relation to legislation providing for unemployment, sickness and invalidity insurance based on compulsory contribution and' which is now claimed to be within or subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces be vested in the dominion government.
My purpose at that time, in moving that the report of the committee on industrial relations be amended, was to have the house take concrete and definite action. It is quite true that in 1929 the unemployment situation was not as serious as it is at the present time, but we knew that as surely as night follows day, cycles of depression follow cycles

Ways and Means
of prosperity. So I wanted the report referred back, with the idea of bringing in some legislation which could be adopted by the provinces exactly as they have adopted the federal legislation in regard to the old age pension measure.
At that time my amendment was ridiculed; lawyers on both sides of the house rose and told me how badly it was drafted, how impossible it was, and how it was ultra vires of the constitution. When the matter came to a vote we saw all the Liberals and Conservatives vote against the amendment, with only eighteen or twenty members of the house supporting it. My amendment was defeated, and that was the last we heard about unemployment insurance for some little time. However, the unemployment situation became worse, and on March 31, 1930, the following year, on going into supply I moved:
-in the opinion of this house the government should take immediate action to deal with the question of unemployment.
Again I raised the question of unemployment insurance.

The house resumed from Wednesday, January 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Church:
That in the opinion of this house Canada should inaugurate at once a national housing, building and reconstruction policy adapted to its circumstances, and that such a policy is an economic and social necessity and in the best interests of the people of our country.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to detain the house for more than a few moments this afternoon
Housing Policy-Mr. Church

he made last night in Montreal that there is to be a reconstruction policy, which I understand from the newspapers will involve some $40,000,000. I am glad also that something is to be done with regard to housing, commensurate with the needs of the country and the ability of the taxpayer to pay, in view of the state of the country's finances. There is no reason why this policy should not be supported by the Progressive and the Liberal parties, for it is good Liberal doctrine. It seems to me that the government in the old country is to be commended. While it is true that it may be called a Labour government, it is supported by the Conservative party there, and it is certainly to be congratulated on the reforms which it is carrying out. I believe all parties in the house should unite and do something to try not only to cure this defect but to help tc remedy this unemployment that is bearing so heavily upon our people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I have supported the resolution of the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Church) from a partly different viewpoint. I am not altogether in favour of every argument he has advanced in support of this resolution, but I have a vivid recollection of 1919 when the then dominion government decided to appropriate an amount of, I think, $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 for the purpose of a housing scheme. The result of this was to give employment to a great number of men. The money was distributed, as I remember, according to population and as a result the government has received back from most, if not all of the provinces, the total amount of the capital expenditure. This scheme at that time produced certain results that were beneficial to the country as a whole.
We must remember, too, that the building industry as such is composed of at least ninety to ninety-five per cent of labour and I say that after careful study of the situation. We have, for instance, the steel industry in Canada which supplies the wants of most of our Canadian building industries. We have the cement industry, the brick industry, the lumber industry and all those others that combine to make a house for an ordinary man in an ordinary situation. In every one of these cases it will be found that on the average the labour costs are at least ninety per cent of the whole. Therefore, any policy that might be enunciated by any government in Great Britain or any other country, would have the advantage of giving employment to the ex-
tent of ninety to ninety-five per cent of the total expenditure.
There is no doubt at the present time the building situation in Canada as in many other countries is at an absolute standstill. We have not the ordinal amount of capital flowing from our insurance companies or from other sources which are willing to accept mortgages at the present mortgage rates. The result is that the building industry in cities like Toronto, Montreal and many others is at an absolute standstill and two and even three families are being crowded into premises which originally were designed to house only one. I am not interested in this proposition except perhaps from this viewpoint, that I represent a riding which is concerned largely with the lumbering industry and partly with the other industries connected with the building program. We also wish to build more freely and under better conditions, just the same as the city of Toronto does. I am sure this is equally true of Montreal, Sorel or any other city in Quebec, and it is equally true in the western provinces. I am desirous of having this government if possible enunciate a policy which will tend to relieve the situation and which will give an impetus to the building of homes for our people throughout the dominion. There is no question about the fact that, as I have already stated, this money will eventually go to the extent of ninety-five per cent into the hands of our wage earners. I can conceive of nothing which would do more to better the present situation than a proposal of this kind.
I represent a riding which is partly lumbering, partly farming. During the winter the farmers depend to a great extent upon the lumbering industry, and this has been cut off, not because of hard times, but simply because the building industry has been strangled by one means or another; and I have no intention of saying what those means are. But I believe if the government would accept a policy of this kind and do what is possible, as was done in 1919, to relieve the housing situation, they would accomplish a great deal and would be doing it in the right way.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Church) for introducing the resolution which is now before the house. Mr. ST-PERE: There is no shortage of houses in Montreal.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext:
I would like to stress the need of good homes in Canada because of the climate in which we live, and while I do not want to advertise our climate as not being a good one, it is such that our people should be able to enjoy the benefit of good warm modern homes whereas about one-half of our houses are not of that type. A large percentage of the people in our part of the country are living in what we call shacks, and a large percentage of those in the cities are living in what are termed slums. The bureau of statistics, I know, has considerable information upon this subject, information that was gathered when the census was taken in 1931. Unfortunately, that information has not yet been made available to us in pamphlet form. I understand it will very soon be available and I regret it has been so long delayed. Of course I realize that is because the bureau has been a little short of help in compiling the statistics in that form. I know there is a need for many more rural homes-and I say "homes" advisedly, because as to many of the places in which our people are living it is a little difficult to call them homes, they are so inadequate. Only five per cent of the farm homes in Canada are equipped with bathrooms with running water. Six hundred and fifty thousand farm homes in Canada should be equipped to-day with modern facilities, and in any housing project which may be started should take cognizance of that situation. In other words, the project should be such that many of these houses in the country could be changed into modern homes. I mean that in addition to building new houses it should be possible to have a scheme for financing the rehabilitation of a lot of houses that now exist.
I have here a few facts gathered by a housing commission in the city of Halifax a few years ago. I placed them on Hansard in March, 1932, and seeing that no steps have been taken, as far as I know, to remedy these conditions I would like to quote two or three of them again. I am sure they are indicative of conditions that exist in other cities of Canada as well. They showed that in one
case, for one room in a cellar occupied by five persons, a monthly rental of $10 was being collected. In another case people were paying $6 a. month for one room in a cellar occupied by seven persons. In another case $12 was being paid for living quarters in the loft of a barn occupied by six persons. Seven rooms were occupied by twenty-eight persons at a rental of $150 per month. In another case two cellar rooms occupied by eight persons cost $10 per month. In one case one dark room with door only was occupied by three persons for which they paid $10 a month. Many other somewhat similar instances are quoted in that report. I say again I do not think this applies only or particularly to the city of Halifax; it is a situation that can be duplicated in many of our cities. I am simply trying to make the point clear that houses are needed both in the cities and in the rural communities. We have in Canada everything necessary for the construction of houses-concrete, brick, stone, lumber; I think all kinds of building material and building hardware is manufactured here. I presume even the window glass can be made in Canada, or if not we certainly could trade wheat with Belgium for it.

Another seven cents goes to workers in the raw materials industries-forests, iron, coal, et cetera. Four cents goes to workers on railroads and trucking for transporting goods et cetera. Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	Mr. Speaker, I want to say how
thoroughly I am in sympathy with this resolution. As I listened to-day to the several speeches made on the address in reply, excellent speeches, that much as I find myself in agreement with the social legislation now proposed, I have become more and more alarmed with regard to the position of the farmer. Many of these proposals, good as they are, are for those other than agriculturists, and unless something is to be done to guarantee to the farmer if not a fixed price at any rate a price level that will take care of the cost of production, including wages for the farmer and all the members of his family who work with him, I really view the future for agriculture with a good deal of misgiving.
The rural buildings in the province of Ontario need repair terribly. I am familiar with this province; as I go over it and see the sections and counties that were really beautiful

Housing Policy-Mr. Mitchell
ten or fifteen years ago, and contrast with that their present condition, I cannot help but become saddened by it, as I am sure other hon. members of this house must be. All hon. members, as politicians, must be familiar with farm houses; some of you must have stayed in them, particularly hon. members who have constituencies which are partly rural. You know without being told how much the farmer is doing without. You know, as I do, something of what he is putting up with, the lack of reasonably good housing, of decent lighting, of sanitary conveniences, of comfortable furniture, of adequate reading material and of almost everything that goes to make up the sum total of human happiness. So, much as I favour the housing program, I want to say as emphatically as possible that any program that does not provide for the repair of such farm buildings as already exist, as well as the installation of conveniences in farm homes, is insufficient. It is a fact that many farmers who are still struggling to pay their debts, who still call themselves independent and who resent any suggestion of what they still call charity, are living below the level of people on relief. That brings me to the question of the cost. The farmers cannot afford much unless farm prices are raised, and I read the speech from the throne in vain for assurance that would give me hope that this is to come about. If farm prices are not raised then any interest rates that the farmer may be required to pay must be very, very low. It seems to me that if the chartered banks can pull figures out of thin air which they call money, there is no reason at all why the dominion government cannot do the same thing. They should be able to lend vast sums of money to municipalities at exceedingly low rates of interest, and I believe this plan would work out better if the municipalities are closer to the people. Mr. Speaker, I should like to make one or two observations with regard to the resolution moved by the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Church). I believe that if he has done nothing else he has made a distinct contribution to the present session of parliament by moving this resolution, which may result in a crystallization of opinion from one end of the dominion to the other as to the vital necessity of a housing policy at least within the confines of the larger centres.
An hon. member representing a Montreal constituency said that there was no shortage of houses in that city. That may be true, but I think it is only fair to say that I know of no city in the dominion that needs a housing policy more than it is needed by the city of Montreal. I do not say that in any spirit of criticism; to a lesser degree the same might be said of the city of Toronto, and from my practical experience in the city of Hamilton I certainly .believe it is needed there.
One of the most important problems confronting us in negotiating any building policy under private enterprise is the enormous lieight to which interest rates have risen in the last three or four years, making it economically unsound to launch a building program of any description. The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) spoke of houses that needed repair. I speak of houses that are .beyond repair. Conditions exist in most of the larger cities of eastern Canada which, in my judgment, constitute a challenge to the vision of those responsible for the housing of our population. Last year I spent some time in England and on the continent, and I was amazed at the real progress that has been made there in connection with housing schemes, most of which have had assistance from the various governments. Even where I lived in England as a boy I noticed a tremendous difference, with the development of garden cities and other developments that were economically sound because they were revenue producing.

Hon. members I think will recall that at the first session of this parliament, the so-called special session, and all subsequent sessions, I stressed very strongly the desirability of the government, in dealing with the problem of unemployment, appointing a national commission or committee, a body that would be representative of the more important industrial and philanthropic interests in the country, of employers and employees, of railway companies, of such organizations as chambers of commerce, the manufacturers' association, the trades and labour congress, the Salvation Army, the Red Cross and bodies of that sort, which national commission would be a body formed for the purpose of administering expenditure of federal appropriations for relief purposes and supervising and linking up all efforts at relieving unemployment and providing work by coordinating whatever might owe its origin to funds provided by the federal government, provincial governments and municipalities or other bodies.
The government at that time, I believe, thought the depression was not going to be of long duration, and, as members will recall, the vote of S20,000,000 was asked for. It was voted in a lump sum without any indication being given to the House of Commons as to how' that money was likely to be spent, other than that it was in the nature of a grant in aid to the provinces in connection with public works which they themselves might undertake. Session after session that same method was adopted of voting large sums of public money. definite, when a bill was passed appropriating public moneys for the construction of public works and public buildings.

I might read again what I read on monday last as the statement of Liberal policy on this matter, as it was outlined at the first session and subsequent sessions and as it was placed on record along with other matters of Liberal policy in one comprehensive Statement in this house on February 27, 1933:
Unemployment of First Concern
The Liberal party believes unemployment is Canada's most urgent national problem. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and myself had the privilege and the pleasure of visiting Great Britain last year. I am sure he was impressed, as I was, with what is to be seen there of the immensely improved conditions" as respects housing for the industrial classes throughout Great Britain. There is nothing quite so much in evidence as to what has been and is being done in the way of improving the living conditions of the people during this period of hard times, as is to be seen in the improved housing conditions. The better housing schemes have served two purposes. Two birds, in other words, have been killed with the one stone; public moneys, in helping to provide employment, have also helped to provide better housing conditions. I had the privilege also of visiting one or two other countries in Europe, and I must say that what I saw, especially in Italy, in the way of what the government had accomplished during this period of unemployment by putting to work unemployed men on housing schemes, park and recreational developments and the improvement of conditions generally in the cities and around the homes of the working classes was the most impressive of anything I saw while abroad.
In the working out of a national housing, building and reconstruction policy, there is no need of any question of jurisdiction arising. I remember at the time that the Prime Minister stated that he did not think any moneys paid out of the federal treasury to the provinces should be supervised even by the auditor general-that it would be an insult to ask that the auditor general be given the right of seeing how federal moneys which had been turned over to the provinces to assist in unemployment relief
[Mr. Mackenzie King i
had been spent. Well, I think the Prime Minister has seen-he has confessed it-that there was enormous waste of public money as a result of failure to adopt that precaution of having all public expenditures out of the federal treasury supervised by the officer of this parliament who has been appointed for that purpose.
Not only has this money been in large part wasted, but many of the municipalities have found themselves well-nigh driven into a position of bankruptcy, simply because for a long time they felt that the only way in which they could get a share of federal or provincial moneys was by agreeing to contribute more for public expenditures on relieving unemployment than they would otherwise have felt they were in a position to afford.
I am sure that a body of the character which I have suggested would have been of great service. It was suggested every session, first at the short session, then at the second, the third, the fourth and the fifth, and now at this sixth session I am going to suggest it again as the proper way of dealing with this question, namely, the appointment of a national commission to supervise the whole matter of the expenditure of public moneys on relief and in providing means of employment. That is the step that should be taken if this work which is nation-wide in extent is to be carried out effectively. It is essentially effective cooperation and coordination in all effort that looks to providing employment that is needed in dealing with a great problem, such as this problem has been all along through these past five years.
During the time of the war, when we had a national patriotic fund to be administered, a national committee was appointed under federal act for the purpose, and the auditor general or a member of his staff was appointed in connection with the supervision of all outlays. Some of the moneys were federal, some were provincial and some were moneys raised by municipalities and voluntary organizations of one character or another. But the whole fund was administered and supervised as one, the actual disbursements being made of course locally, but the fund ran into many millions of dollars. When the committee's work was completed, and the auditor general's department made its report on the expenditure of the moneys every cent of the moneys contributed from different sources was accounted for. As far as I recall, and I was a member of the national committee, there was not a single dollar of money that had been contributed to the patriotic fund which was not

The result is that there have been constructed in Ontario, in cities, towns, in organized districts such as villages and what are called rural communities, in counties, large undertakings to which all three have contributed. To suggest at any time to the province of Ontario that some commission would determine how muni-
cipalities or towns or other communities or the province itself should expend given money is a matter to which they have not listened favourably; at least they did not in my time. They may have changed.
In Quebec the greatest difficulty was of course in the city of Montreal. There a commission was set up by the province, but the manner in which it administered its duties was not at all times satisfactory to those who created it, and they have had many difficulties to overcome. In the western provinces commissions were set up for the purpose of determining how assistance could be granted, to what extent work might be possible, and I shall point out that in the part of the country where unemployment was very noticeable, that is because of crop failures and other conditions that obtained, there were seasonal difficulties, very cold weather, which made it impossible to carry on building and many other operations that could be carried on in warmer climates. A construction program was the first one the late Senator Robertson initiated and organized from one end of the country to the other. He provided1 for the elimination of level crossings on railways, which he hoped might do much to provide employment and do away with a common danger which we all recognize. That did not give employment to the extent that was expected, and the expenditures were not in the main, shall I say, very much appreciated by the communities in which they were made. Then the question of the construction of highways seemed to be the only method by which public moneys could afford employment to the class which appeared to be at that time, because of lack of crops, suffering very considerably. The result was that roads were constructed; that is, assistance was given to the province to enable roads to be constructed, and from Manitoba to the Rocky mountains a considerable number of miles of road were constructed and improved, giving employment to men, teams, and in every way doing something to lessen the evils of unemployment. In British Columbia the Parks branch expanded the program that had been outlined by our predecessors in office and in the other national parks the same thing took place. The result was that a considerable number of people found employment, but in all these cases the provinces outside the national parks claimed the right to exercise their jurisdiction and to determine where, so far as it might be possible, work could best be done for the purpose of providing employment. I do say to the right hon. gentleman that there were no

Housing Policy-Mr. Bennett
greater abuses, having regard to the amounts involved in the expenditures of the moneys to which the dominion contributed, than there has been in respect to old age pensions.

speechtext:
That is not
correct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext: I am bound to say that it is.
