speechtext: What is more, the investigation we have made shows the situation to be even worse in regard to old age pensions than it is in regard to unemployment relief, except in a few isolated cases where laxity was so apparent as to necessitate criminal proceedings being taken, not by the dominion but by the communities themselves that were defrauded of their moneys by those receiving benefits.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext: Did the right hon. gentleman himself not find it necessary two years ago to pass an order in council providing that the auditor general should audit these very moneys that were being handed over to the provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext:
An order in council was passed with respect to public works and undertakings, not of the type to which the right hon. gentleman has referred, but of the type where contributions were made to the cost of the ultimate undertaking providing that the auditor general should examine and determine whether the moneys which had been granted were properly expended. I was able to point out to the right hon. gentleman by the production of a sample sheet that had been approved by the comptroller of the treasury that no moneys thus expended were expended so far as the issuing of the cheque was concerned unless and until there appeared upon the sheet the initials of two auditors of the auditor general's department as a preaudit of their correctness, a certificate by the municipality itself that the moneys were expended in the municipality, and a certificate by the province in which the moneys were expended, so that whatever might happen, if there were fraud or deception practised, the dominion would be always in a position to secure from the province or municipality any moneys that had been improperly used. I am informed that there was no single case in which the comptroller of the treasury issued a cheque in which there was not, prior to the cheque being issued, a certificate not only of the province but of the lesser organization,
whether it be a town or a city or a municipality, in which the money had been expended, as to the correctness of the expenditure. I mention that because in connection with matters of that kind, it is quite clear the situation is entirely different from the granting of, let us say, S100 for municipal aid. If there is need for municipal aid of $100, it is obvious the manner in which the municipality may expend that money is not a matter into which the auditor general could inquire, except to see that the municipality had properly received it, if it were a grant in aid.
A construction program with respect to roads, with respect to railway crossings and other matters was settled and determined by the late Senator Robertson on the first tour he made to the Pacific coast and back. During that fall a substantial number of men were employed at that kind of work, but of course when the cold weather came on such work could not proceed in the prairie provinces. In every case, however, the next year and the next, the character of the undertakings was determined by conferences with the provinces.
The difference between the suggestion which the right hon. gentleman makes and the policy pursued by the government is this; we endeavoured by cooperation with the provinces -not having any contact with the municipalities, they being the creatures of the provincial legislatures-to assist the provinces in the discharge of their duty, having regard to the national character of the problems with which we had to deal. The right hon. gentleman suggests that a commission or committee might have been set up which would be able to deal with all the provinces. We believed that the problem in each province was somewhat different, and that the provincial governments and local authorities cooperating with the dominion could determine how the problem should be dealt with, what works should be done, and moneys expended, by agreement between the provinces and the dominion better than by any commission that might be appointed.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext:
I am afraid my right hon. friend, in making a comparison between his plan and mine, if I may use that expression, has not caught the significance of what I have suggested. I have never suggested that a commission should take out of the hands of the federal government its obligations beyond supervising and administering in part federal expenditures of public employment relief moneys in accordance with a definite plan. What I have suggested is that there should be a national commission which would cooperate with the federal government,

Housing Policy-Mr. Bennett
with the provincial governments and with the municipalities, which would endeavour to coordinate the efforts of all and which would report its doings and recommendations in a manner that all these bodies would have a complete picture of all public efforts for the purpose of providing employment and affording relief with a view to having these coordinated, on a voluntary basis of course. Being in a position to say on what conditions federal relief moneys would become available to the provinces and municipalities, and how their expenditure should be audited, such a commission would have little difficulty in effecting coordination.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext: I am sure the right hon. gentleman realizes that it is not in accord with the general rules of the house that he should make another speech in the midst of mine.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext: But if my right hon. friend is going to state what my policy is I must be permitted to correct him if he states it wrongly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext: I am content to leave myself entirely in the hands of the house as to whether I have not correctly stated it. 1 listened with much attention to the right hon. gentleman. He stated that he thought there should be a commission or committee, and the duty of that committee would be to coordinate the efforts of the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext: Supervise everything, administer federal relief funds and do what it could to coordinate the several activities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext:
In other words they would be a fifth wheel to the coach. I did suggest that to deprive the provinces of their powers, to endeavour, by voluntary effort, if you will, to determine how each province should expend its money, was something that the provinces did not indicate any desire or willingness to agree to. They felt that the problem was primarily theirs, although we were giving them assistance, and they were willing to discuss and consider and determine what was best and most urgent and most desirable to be done and how their public moneys as well as ours could best be expended. That was a recognition of their position as sovereign legislatures within the scope of their activities; at the same time the dominion was discharging its obligation to them by giving the assistance I have indicated. That was a recognition of the right of the provinces to continue their activities. It is under that

power that Saskatchewan continues to exercise its powers, contending that they can do it better, more reasonably-and I might add, more politically-than could otherwise be done.
Then there came the position in the province of Quebec. That province contended that they knew far more about the immediate necessities for road construction and various undertakings that should be gone forward with in the province at a particular time than any commission could learn, because a commission must necessarily turn to the provincial government to obtain the information in question. Any commission, however well informed, would never be quite as well informed as the government itself. So the government undertook the responsibility of coordinating its efforts. I should like this to be clearly understood: in every instance where works were undertaken there was an agreement indicating that the province and the dominion had arrived at a conclusion that the given undertaking should be gone on with and that the dominion would make a contribution of a given amount to the cost and the province would determine what it should pay. As 1 say, sometimes municipalities, the rich province of Ontario for instance, made large contributions because they were getting necessary undertakings constructed or completed in a manner that lessened the obligation which would otherwise have been imposed on the ratepayers. To the extent that they received assistance from the dominion or the province the obligation on the ratepayers of the municipality was lessened. When you look at the returns already tabled you will find that in a rich old province such as Ontario they spent very much more money relatively than other provinces, and obtained larger sums from the dominion because their municipalities were in sufficiently good circumstances financially to enable them to undertake such works. The province fixed a figure in all cases that they would give in the way of assistance, either a percentage of the cost of the entire undertaking or a percentage of the labour cost. And in every instance the cabinet determined, the minister having first made a recommendation of what he thought should be done in the way of payment by the dominion, to assist in works of that kind. Of course in unorganized territories where work could not be carried on and where the province had the burden of direct relief, they sought and obtained from the dominion assistance from time to time, sometimes through the medium of a commission which they themselves set up, sometimes directly without

Housing Policy-Mr. Bennett
the intervention of a commission, the province itself assuming the responsibility. But in every case there has been agreement between the province and the dominion. In every case the dominion has taken the position that it could not deal with the municipalities as such, for the municipalities were the creature of the legislatures and the only contact between the dominion and the municipalities was through the provincial governments that called them into being.
That has resulted in very large numbers of public works and undertakings being constructed. When hon. gentlemen study the returns that have been filed they will be amazed, as I have been, to find the extent to which in the old municipalities of various parts of Canada sewer works, streets and sidewalks have been constructed and repairs undertaken; and they have also dealt with, shall I say, some factors of the housing problem. But we did not feel that we were in a position financially during those days to undertake any large scheme of housing such as had been contemplated in Canada in 1919, or in Great Britain. Necessarily many things that one would like to have done could npt be done because of the restrictions imposed upon us by our financial position, largely because with the accentuation of the depression, the slackening of earnings by the Canadian National railway system imposed a larger burden upon the taxpayers to meet the interest charges upon securities guaranteed by the dominion. That is a fact.
Now conditions have improved. Last year we offered to the house a public works program based upon two facts: one being that conditions were improving; the other that the increased price of gold, with the corresponding application of the principle unanimously adopted at the world economic conference as to the extent to which metallic coverage should be provided for our currency, enabled us to offer a program involving an expenditure of forty to fifty million dollars for public works. I say, as I said last night, that it has had a very excellent effect. It has stimulated business and improved credit conditions. But the full effect of the works will not be felt this year, because the preparation of plans and designs and preparation of the sites for the work has taken time, but all this and the acquisition of materials has gone on and conditions have greatly improved.
Now the question is what shall be done with respect to housing. It may surprise the right hon. gentleman, as it surprised me, I may say very frankly, to learn that with respect to one city we were very anxious to try out a form of tenement construction that certainly
appealed very strongly to me. It was of concrete and stone, with a central heating plant; water, gas and light all were provided from a central point, and streets were laid out in an orderly fashion. But to our surprise petitions came to us asking that we should not go forward with the work, because it might interfere with the renting of private properties in the city in question, and stating that the time was not ripe to carry forward a housing program of that character.
This afternoon it was suggested in this house that painting, glazing and the improvement of the exterior as well as the interior of many of our farm houses would be desirable. I wholly agree, but there are many farmers in this country who, being thrifty souls, would not care to incur the financial obligations involved in connection with that work. I say that very frankly, because that suggestion has been contained in statements that have been sent to me from time to time with respect to the matter. But the government realized its obligation and, as will be recalled, set aside a sum of money for the purpose of painting, repairing, glazing and putting into proper condition all the public buildings owned by the crown. Commencing at Vancouver and going through to Cape Breton, that work was carried on. All the necessary work could not be accomplished, but most of it was done, and the effect upon the communities was very considerable. People who had the means themselves began to make their places look a little better, to replace the broken windows, repair the sills and put the houses in better condition. But when it comes to the question of telling individuals that you wish them to make changes, either inside or outside their buildings, on the part of most Canadians there is a tendency to say, " We are the best judges as to the extent of the money that we should spend, or the amount of the debts we should incur."

subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext: They do not like state interference.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext:
They are perfectly willing to be interfered with provided it does not cost them anything; when it comes to the point of paying for it, then it is a different matter.
Now let me proceed, if I may do so without becoming tedious, to point out the position with respect to housing. It is rather a reflection upon us, is it not, that a new country such as this should be talking about housing and slum conditions? It is rather a reflection upon our civilization, according to my view of things, that less than seventy-five years after becoming a dominion we

Housing Policy-Mr. Bennett
should be talking about slum conditions. As one of the hon. members was speaking this afternoon I recalled a conversation I had many years ago with the secretary of the late Bonar Law. She had been bom in Poland, and she said, " Nothing has more impressed me than the fact that, for some strange reason, we never seem able to get away from slums." She added, " Do you realize that the east part of the city of London was completely wiped out by fire in the closing part of the seventeenth century, but that now the worst slums in London are to be found in the area that was then burned clear? Somehow or other slums have a way of growing up." She went on to say that some of the younger generation had given the matter a good deal of thought but had not been able to arrive at any conclusion. I recall also something else that was said at that moment; she said that for some reason slums are usually to be found in the east section of cities. I do not know how correct that is, but that is the observation that was made to me at that time.
In the cities of Toronto, Montreal and Winnipeg-even a new city like that-as well as in some of our older communities such as the city of Halifax, which was mentioned this afternoon, there are buildings which, in my judgment, are not of the type that our people should occupy, from the standpoint of health and happiness. How is that situation to be overcome? In days gone by private capital was always ready and willing to embark on the construction of buildings, because usually that has been a very profitable investment. In the old country it has been one of the favourite forms of investment, but it has not been so in latter days, for reasons into which I need not go this evening. At all events, in 1919, we made up our minds that we would supply the provinces with certain sums of money to enable them, as was their constitutional duty, to deal with these problems. In Saint John, New Brunswick, a city of one hundred and fifty years old or more, there are certain slum clearances going on now. In the city of Halifax, as the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) might have recalled this afternoon, a great disaster occurred, and the conditions that obtained in connection with those buildings that were not completely levelled were somewhat different from the normal conditions prevailing in other communities.
What are we to do about it? That is the real problem. The commission appointed by His Honour the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario went into the matter rather fully and,

as the right hon. gentleman has said a very admirable report was made. I was appalled, however, to find-I am now speaking subject to correction; perhaps my memory is not quite as good as it should be-that the report suggests that the sum of S12,000.000 would be required to provide proper dwelling houses for a certain class in that community who now live in buildings that should be condemned, and that this amount would not be self liquidating. Therefore we have two conditions to deal with. The first is the condition where you have the investment self liquidating. In that case if you set up proper machinery and the money is advanced at a reasonable rate of interest, provision is made for amortization and the properties will pay for themselves in a given number of years. That number of years should be the usual expectation of life of the structure, brick or stone or wood as it may be, with the amortization based upon a given percentage being paid from year to year, so that at the end of the period the building stands free and is supposed to be still in a reasonably decent condition allowing for both obsolescence and depreciation.
That is a simple condition; there is not a tremendous amount of difficulty in dealing with that. It can be done in one of two ways. It can be done in the manner in which we have heretofore dealt with it, namely by securing for the provinces a certain sum of money at low interest rates to enable them to deal with the matter at first hand, or we can set up a commission to deal with it ourselves. It does not seem to me that it was ever intended to be the function of a national government to deal with matters of that kind in the communities. Therefore I still think the method adopted by the government of 1919 or 1920 was the sound method. As a matter of fact inquiries have been made by the government during the last few months, especially in view of the reports coming from Montreal, whence we have received very excellent suggestions looking towards the establishment of homes with little bits of land attached to them. It seems to me that, however small it may be, if there is an area in which a kitchen garden can flourish, with room for a few flowers in front, it adds greatly to the happiness of the persons who have to live in those homes. Similar suggestions have come from other cities in Canada, and of course the condition in Vancouver is well known. They have their difficulties in connection with clearing land when you go out certain distances from the city, but the land close to Vancouver I think may be said to be fairly clear and available for housing purposes.

Housing Policy-Mr. Bennett
The second case is one presenting much more difficulty; it is that class of case which is not self liquidating in which we know perfectly well that, with the standard of wages that has prevailed for the last fifteen, twenty, twenty-five or thirty years, it would not be possible to provide the artisan with a dwelling that we think would be decent, on which he would be able to pay the rental necessary in order to liquidate the cost. That is a different problem altogether. It involves a contribution by the state which will not be repaid and which is a voluntary effort made by the central or provincial power, as the case may be, to add to the happiness and contentment of those who inhabit a certain type of dwelling.
I have a proposal to make. We have given a good deal of thought to this matter, and have received a very large number of suggestions. Obviously no government can adequately deal with all of them. That is the reason I am suggesting that we set up some body which would be able to cull through the suggestions and make recommendations to the government. I purpose placing the matter entirely in the hands of the house, and suggest either the selection of a committee to examine into the matter or that the committee on banking and commerce examine into and make a report to the house, having regard to the conditions to which I have referred which have not to do with the financial side of it, and also with the financial side as well. Whichever view the house thinks desirable the government is only too anxious to accede to.
For the moment I suggest that the hon. member withdraw his motion, and I say to him that I will prepare a proper resolution of which notice will be given to refer the matter either to the committee on banking and commerce or to a select committee. Sometimes there are difficulties in connection with a select committee, and it may be found easier to handle the matter with a standing committee where from time to time all members may attend. However we shall be glad to do whatever the house thinks most desirable.
In a new country such as ours this is an important problem, because we cannot afford to permit a condition develop in Canada such as has obtained, for instance, in the old city of Glasgow. That may be taken as a very good illustration of what I mean. If the condition which developed in Glasgow had been curbed at the start it would not have grown to such large proportions. If we take hold of the matter now, while we have not at the moment all the resources necessary
to enable us to do all we may desire to do, we believe we shall be able to grapple with it in such a way as to make a continuance of slum conditions impossible, and certainly to prevent any increase of the kind of tenement and small buildings to which reference has been made to-day.
I have one word more to say with respect to public works and undertakings. Obviously we cannot deal with these matters on a very large scale. We have dealt with them from two standpoints. The first standpoint is the extent to which employment may be given directly or indirectly. When I use the word "indirectly" I refer to materials which have to do with the construction and carrying on of undertakings, and to the primary and secondary and other industries connected with it. Closely-nay, I might say almost inevitably linked to that factor must be the second one, namely the necessity for the undertaking. I think if my right hon. friend and hon. members of this house will look through the list of public works and undertakings authorized last year, and any additions which may be made to that list, they will realize how necessary every undertaking was, not only for the community affected but for the country as a whole. There were wharves, breakwaters and constructions of that kind required. These were really essential to the well being of the communities, but for obvious reasons we had not heretofore been able to deal with them. That is the attitude of the government with respect to these matters, and we are entirely in the hands of the house as to whether the banking and commerce committee or a select committee should deal with the problem and make a report. We will be satisfied to place it in the hands of whichever body will best serve the interests of our country at this time.
Before resuming my seat may I say that my right hon. friend is hardly fair in his reference to the patriotic fund. The patriotic fund w'as one of which the Minister of Finance was honorary treasurer and the auditor general honorary auditor. It had nothing to do in a public way in any shape or form with the conduct of the business of the country, but was a fund created by the government, and largely by private subscriptions. In the ultimate administration-for in the part of the country in which I live I personally had something to do with it-individuals themselves were dealt with by a committee which was appointed. The honorary auditor, the auditor general himself saw that all the moneys received from every source were available for the expenditures which were made, but he did not undertake

Housing Policy-Mr. Bennett
at any time to examine as to whether or not John Smith who in Calgary was said to have received a given sum of money had actually received it, nor did he satisfy himself as to its necessity. The committee made a report upon that, and that report was acted upon. The general executive here in Ottawa dealt with the large problems of policy, the determination of the extent to which moneys which had been paid might meet the demands made upon the fund, with the interest which had accrued. As the right hon. gentleman knows, the fund is now practically exhausted. However it has been so splendidly administered and has been so great a source of assistance to those who otherwise would not be cared for that I think we may all look upon its administration with great pride. It was administered not as a public fund, but as a public trust for those who received moneys. I was honorary treasurer for the period I happened to be Minister of Finance, and the present Minister of Finance is now honorary treasurer of the fund.

It was a public body

speechtext:
Before the right hon. gentleman closes his remarks may I offer a suggestion? It seems to me that a select committee composed of the various representatives of larger centres in which the need is greatest would be a proper committee to set up. But in case the government, after an
rMr. Bennett.]
understanding with the opposition, would prefer a standing committee, it seems to me that the committee on industrial relations would be better qualified than the committee on banking and commerce.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for Labelle for his observations. I shall submit a resolution to the house and leave it for the chamber itself to determine whether or not the standing committee I mention shall be chosen, the one mentioned by the hon. member or a select standing committee. I think there are many parts of the country in which the matter is not of very great importance, but certainly the larger centres are deeply interested. If a select committee will best serve the purpose the motion will be for such a committee. However I shall offer the motion in a form which will enable, shall I say, the opinion of the majority of members ultimately to prevail.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL POLICY OF BUILDING AND RECONSTRUCTION AS ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL NECESSITY

I shall gladly accept the suggestion made by the Prime Minister, and ask permission to withdraw the motion.
Motion (Mr. Church) withdrawn.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ADOPTION OP POLICY IN COOPERATION WITH THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 beg to move, seconded by Miss Macphail:
That, in the opinion of this house, the federal government should adopt a definite health policy which could be carried on in cooperation with the provincial governments.
A year ago, Mr. Speaker, I introduced a resolution in this house along somewhat similar lines. At that time, however, I suggested that the resolution should go to the committee on industrial and international relations for consideration and report. The Minister of Health at that time, although having no objection to the principle of my resolution, objected to its going to that committee or to any committee and therefore refused to consent to the resolution passing the house. Although I believe the minister at that time was entirely wrong, nevertheless in introducing the subject this session I have omitted all reference to a committee of this house so that that objection cannot be put forward, and in the hope that the resolution will be accepted by this chamber.
There is no doubt in my mind that hon. members in this house appreciate to the full the importance of this subject of public health. It is brought home to us when we realize that during the last six years we have

Health Policy-Mr. Spencer
had the subject brought before the house no less than seven times. It is true I was responsible for bringing it before the house in 1930. 1931 and 1934, and I have no apology to offer to the house for introducing it again this session.
It is recognized, I know, that the matter of public health comes under the jurisdiction of both federal and provincial authorities. The British North America Act, by which we are governed, does not indicate under which government this subject shall come, but it has been the practice of the provincial governments very largely to carry the load, and they have spent a great deal of money in the carrying on of public health work. But although nothing is said in the British North America Act as to whose is the responsibility, we recognize that consideration is given in the act to questions which are interprovincial in character. Under the act these come under federal jurisdiction. We have to recognize that sickness and disease do not stop at any provincial boundary, and I therefore feel that the federal government has a definite responsibility in this matter.
Studying this subject of public health the other day I came to realize that there were at least five problems with regard to public health that really should come under federal jurisdiction: such sicknesses as tuberculosis and cancer; the prevention and control of insanity; venereal diseases; child and maternal welfare. I appreciate the fact that certain grants have been made in past years and are made to a certain extent to-day in connection with these matters, but the load of responsibility and expense has been left very largely to the provinces. The federal government takes over complete control of immigration, complete control of the examination of immigrants coming into this country, and has spent public funds lavishly in this regard in past years. That being so, I feel I am justified in suggesting that child welfare and maternal welfare should come largely under federal jurisdiction.
Last year I pointed out that it is only at a time of great crisis that the country recognizes the enormous loss which it suffers through not having a proper health system. I pointed out that during the great war it was not until volunteers were called for that we had a situation on our hands that showed us quite clearly that owing to the lack of a proper health policy a very large number of our people were not physically, if mentally fit. Of the volunteers who came forward no less than one-third were unfit for service at the front. When it became necessary to put
conscription in force the figures were still worse, because of those called to the colours no less than two-thirds were found to be unfit for military service. This meant the loss of a huge sum of money running into millions of dollars which might have been saved if we had had in effect prior to that time a thoroughly workable and coordinated health policy.
I also pointed out last year that over 46,000 Canadian children die every year under the age of five years. This in itself is a tragedy. Everyone will admit that it is the most terrible tragedy we have to face, and I am sure the whole house will be one in feeling that a stop should be put to this toll of death; because from the very best information we can get, a large proportion, if not the majority, of these deaths could have been avoided if preventive measures had been taken.
From the best figures I can get I would say that sickness costs Canada approximately $300,000,000 a year, and when we take into account the indirect loss, the value of the lives lost-for each life has a value- the loss is upwards of a billion dollars. But let us take the figure of $300,000,000 as the direct loss through sickness. We are spending on public health through all governmental sources, federal, provincial and municipal, the sum of only $6,000,000. Surely it would be real economy to spend more in preventive measures, and so cut down this enormous cost of sickness-in other words, reduce the high cost of sickness.
I take it that most members will agree with me when I say that sickness and death are inversely proportionate to the amount of money spent on health measures. Society, it seems to me, has two responsibilities with regard to sickness: one is the adoption of curative measures, and the other is the adoption of preventive measures. Up to the present time we have paid more attention to curative than to preventive measures, and we have not achieved the results which I hope will ensue when more attention is paid to prevention. When we recognize that there are no less than 180,000 people sick daily in this country-sick enough to prevent them from working-it will be seen that we have a great problem on our hands and one that should be faced. If it were faced I am sure we should get splendid returns. We spend more in curing people than it would be necessary to spend in preventive medicine, and many people owing to the high cost of medical attendance have to go without attention owing to the high cost of medical care. I

Health Policy-Mr. Spencer
we have to look at this matter of health not only from the human point of view, which I think should be intensified, but also from that of business, and from the latter alone, so far as spending money on health is concerned, we can increase the dividends enormously over what we have done in the past. There is something wrong, for instance, when in Canada some 25,000 children die each year before they are a year old, and most of them from preventable sicknesses.
Before I close I want to congratulate the various provinces, some of which are doing better work than others, on the work they have done. As I said before, they are all handicapped in the matter of finances. I hold in my hand a magazine entitled Health, published, I believe, under the auspices of the Canadian Social Hygiene Council. This is a body of private people, well-wishers for the better health of the Canadian people, who through a very considerable volunteer effort have probably done more than most other organizations to bring before the public and the different governments, the necessity of doing better and better work with regard to the health problem. I understand the Prime Minister some time ago suggested that at the next dominion-provincial conference the subject of health should be considered. I have here a statement from the Hon. J. A. Faulkner, Minister of Health for Ontario; another from Mr. Taschereau, Premier of Quebec; another from Hon. W. J. P. MacMillan, Premier and Minister of Public Health of Prince Edward Island; another from the Hon. F. R. Davis, Minister of Public Health of Nova Scotia; another from Hon. Weir, Provincial Secretary of British Columbia; another from Mr. Bracken, Premier of Manitoba; another from Hon. George Hoadley, Minister of Health for Alberta; another from Hon. Uhrieh, Minister of Health in Saskatchewan, and lastly, one from Hon. H. I. Taylor, Minister of Health and Labour of New Brunswick. They all submit that this is the proper place in which to bring this subject up. They all make worthwhile statements in regard to the necessity of giving more attention to health, but I am only going to take time to quote a wire from one of them, which is very similar to the rest. In reply to a wire asking whether they were agreeable to taking up the matter of health at this suggested conference, Mr. Weir, Provincial Secretary of British Columbia sent this telegram:
The government of British Columbia is anxious to cooperate with the federal authorities in the promotion of public health which we regard as the very cornerstone of national well being and hence as a matter of national
[Mr Spencer.]
responsibility. Sporadic provincial attacks on cancer, venereal disease, tuberculosis, mental hygiene and child welfare, for instance, can never be so effective as coordinated measures under enlightened federal leadership. From a standpoint of scientific public health provincial boundary lines have little significance. It would be premature to discuss the possible details of health insurance before the meeting of the conference.
I have referred to these letters because they show that those responsible for health in the different provinces are all anxious and of one accord in their desire to do something with the aid of the federal government to bring about a national health plan. I therefore trust that the resolution that I have submitted will be favourably considered by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Sutherland) and that in the course of this evening it will be accepted by the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. M. SUTHERLAND (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subsubtopic: PROPOSED ADOPTION OP POLICY IN COOPERATION WITH THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
I have
listened with attention to the very interesting summary of health matters made by the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Spencer). I congratulate him on the interest that he has taken in this important subject during his time here as a representative of his constituency. I think, however, he has painted rather too gloomy a picture of the health of the people of Canada, because as a general rule I believe the health of our people will compare very favourably with that of those of other nations. No matter what is done, sickness cannot be entirely prevented; it is going to be with us no matter what measures are taken, or by what bodies. But it is also undoubtedly true that preventive steps have been and will be taken with a very beneficial effect indeed on the health of the nation. It has been said that good health is an individual's greatest asset, and that the health of its citizens is a nation's greatest care. I think that is true.
There has been a great change in the practice of medicine since the middle of the last century. This seems an excellent opportunity to glance over those changes, and I think the time spent in so doing may be profitable, because we are representatives of all parts of the country and represent many professions and callings. Therefore I should like for a few moments to indicate the changes that have taken place in the conduct of medical affairs during recent years.
Anesthesia, perhaps the greatest boon that has come to the surgeon and his patient, was discovered only during the last century. Antiseptic and aseptic surgery also came into being within the memory of almost everyone here. These developments have made pos-

Health Policy-Mr. Sutherland
sible a tremendous advance in the treatment of disease. The advances that have been made in medical science have been along three lines; that of prevention, that of diagnosis and that of treatment. In the field of prevention perhaps the greatest advances have been made in the case of some of the diseases mentioned by the hon. member. Tuberculosis, diphtheria and smallpox were at one time prevalent in this country, and one of the outstanding examples of what science has done in the prevention of disease is the combating of yellow fever which was formerly very prevalent in southern countries. I should like to give a few figures as to the improvement there has been lately with regard to some of these diseases-I am taking recent years, because compared with fifty years back there would be a tremendous change. The improvement is continuing: every year there has been a change for the better, as is shown by the following figures:

Another disease which the hon. member mentioned, which is a scourge of very young children, and often leaves severe complications is whooping cough. The figures on that
are as follows:
