These figures show that the continuous fight which is being put up by public bodies and public health institutions throughout the country is producing most excellent results.
In the realm of diagnosis there has also been very great improvement. On the early and accurate diagnosis of disease depends the treatment and, very largely, the outcome. In that field science has made great advances. It has given us the X-ray, which is of inestimable value. The microscope has made possible numerous refinements of diagnosis applying to many diseases, and is of the greatest benefit in the cure of the patient. As to treatment, there have also been great changes both in methods and in instruments used. In the treatment of tuberculosis and pneumonia the idea of the patient getting plenty of fresh air has saved many lives. Then take cancer; the discovery that radium, properly used in properly selected cases, is of great benefit to those suffering from cancer has been one of the most important and most beneficial discoveries ever made in connection with that disease. Another discovery, per-82582-12
fected in our own country, was the use of insulin, which was developed by Doctor Banting in Toronto. A comparison of figures showing the deaths from coma in diabetes is instructive, and shows the great advances that have been made in the treatment of that disease. In 1898, which was long before insulin was heard of, sixty per cent of those dying from diabetes went into a coma before death. The coma is the toxic stage, and in those days there was practically no hope of getting a patient out of that condition. In the period from 1930 to 1933, however, less than five per cent of those dying went into that incurable stage of coma, and as the use of this important medical agent is further perfected undoubtedly the results will be even more beneficial.
So in those three great departments of medicine, prevention, diagnosis and treatment, great changes for the better have been made. The advances I have mentioned have almost revolutionized the practice of medicine. My father was a doctor; I have always lived in a doctor's home, and I know that in the old days practically all the medical attention given throughout the country was given by the general practitioner. That situation has greatly changed, however; it has become almost impossible for the general practitioner to keep himself acquainted with all the new products and inventions of science. Just here, perhaps, I might digress to pay a tribute to one general practitioner who has brought high honour to himself, to his profession and to Canada. I refer to Doctor Dafoe, of northern Ontario. One day he went out on a case which appeared to be a very ordinary incident in the life of a country doctor, but he conducted himself so well that he earned a victory never before earned by an obstetrician in the history of the world. To bring those five northern babies up to the age of seven or eight months, as he has done, has been a wonderful feat, and as Minister of Health I wish to express to Doctor Dafoe the great admiration of the medical profession as a whole for the wonderful work he has done.
These new conditions that I have indicated have necessitated new agencies in dealing with disease. One that I might mention is the public health nurse. In most of our cities and towns at the present time we have the public health nurse. In Ontario part of her salary is paid by the province and part by the municipality. She pays regular visits to the schools and makes suggestions as to whether or not the children need treatment. The work that has been done by these nurses has been very beneficial and very protective.



Health Policy-Mr. Sutherland
I take it that the mover of the resolution would like to see something done along these lines, only to a greater extent.
Then there is another public body which renders useful service to the sick throughout the country; I refer to the Victorian Order of Nurses. I think perhaps from a doctor's standpoint the Victorian Order of Nurses does more good and is of more actual benefit to the sick people than any other similar institution in the country. Personally I regard that body as doing very excellent work throughout the country.
Then in certain parts of the country we have health units, which were mentioned by the hon. member who moved the resolution. This is another means of medical activity which I value very highly. In a general way the object of a health unit is to extend public health activities to rural districts, so that they really have a clinic available to them to give advice on medical subjects, principally in the preventive sphere. They educate the public with regard to the best methods of preventing disease. As they move about the homes they see improvements that might be made, perhaps in connection with drainage or something along that line, and they also have to do with the children both of the pre-school and the school age. They visit the schools and examine conditions there; they also examine the younger children and give advice to the parents as to what might be done for the children. Another important function of the health clinic is the education of mothers, both before children are born and in the postnatal period, as to the care that should be exercised. That work, in certain parts of the country, has had wonderful results. Probably the province of Quebec has made greater advances in connection with health units than have been made in any other part of the country, and I think that province is to be congratulated on the way it has supported the movement and on the benefits that have accrued from it.
Those associated with these health units also carry on a campaign against the various contagious diseases and, in cooperation with the doctors of the community, epidemics can be stamped out much more quickly than was possible in the past. They also have to do with the distribution of sera and vaccines. They inoculate the children against smallpox and diphtheria, and in some parts of the country, as a result of the work of these health clinics, practically all the children have been inoculated against that disease, with most beneficial results.
The great strides that have been made in connection with medicine have gradually made the people feel that they must cooperate in
(Mr. Sutherland.]
order to get the full benefit from these advances, since a serious and prolonged disease is very costly. Perhaps the first step in the way of cooperation in order to secure medical attention was made by the fraternal societies. In practically every town and village throughout Ontario there were one or two fraternal societies which, as a part of the benefits extended to their members, included the free services of a doctor. Sometimes that worked well, sometimes not so well, but it indicated the effort being made by the people to cooperate along these lines. Then various large industries throughout the country started schemes of mutual assistance, the workman putting up so much of the money and the industry supplying the remainder. In that way the members of the industry, the workmen, had an opportunity to get medical assistance without the financial burden being too heavy.
Great advances have been made both in the number of hospitals in Canada and the efficiency with which they have helped to combat disease. Most hon. members can recall the time when there were very few hospitals; particularly those living in the rural sections found it difficult to obtain hospital treatment. To-day with the exception of some few rural districts the country is well provided with hospitals. At the present time there are in Canada 893 modern fully equipped hospitals with 87,645 beds. The hospitals are of various types, including maternity, pediatric, orthopaedic, isolation, and other kinds which I shall not take the time to mention. In addition we have in Canada to-day 59 mental hospitals. The hon. member who preceded me mentioned preventive treatment in mental cases. May I say to him that that is a science the study of which to-day is more or less in its infancy but undoubtedly there is a great opportunity for further research. Constant effort is being made to treat mental troubles in their early stages. Every person connected with the medical profession is hoping that work along that line will be carried to a successful conclusion.
Throughout the country, beginning in the small municipalities, we have boards of health. In the small municipalities the boards of health are sometimes good, sometimes not so good, and in my judgment sometimes useless. Particularly in townships where by law they are forced to have a medical health officer I believe a great deal of money is wasted. In many instances they have some official who is medical health officer in name only, who gets practically no salary and who cannot be expected to do and in fact does not do very much.
I am of the opinion that there must be a development such as was mentioned by the

Health Policy-Mr. Sutherland
hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) and to which I have referred, namely that of health units. I believe that if the money which has been spent for the various township bodies in western Ontario had been lumped and doctors and nurses had been employed the effect would have been much better.
On the other hand in our larger cities we have some first class boards of health doing creditable work. Many people say that the city of Toronto has the best health department in the world. If that is not quite so it is undoubtedly true that Toronto ranks very high in health protection. Many people who are interested in preventive medicine have come from different parts of the world to that city in order to learn firsthand their method of working. The provinces are doing excellent work, some better than others. The hon. member has referred to Alberta; I am in a position to know that the health departments in that province are doing splendid wTork and are preparing to take still further steps to improve the conditions under which their citizens are living. Most of the provinces are to be congratulated upon the excellent work they have been doing.
I should like now to refer to the subject of periodical health examination. If it were possible to have people take those examinations the results would be excellent, but of the 245 members who compose this House of Commons I venture to suggest no more than ten per cent have an annual examination, or even one every two years. They do not lack the money, but they do lack interest. I believe that is characteristic of well-to-do people throughout the country. In general practice I have found that there are very few who make a practice of periodical examinations. I am convinced that such examinations would be of the greatest benefit but we cannot go out on the street and force people to go into doctors' offices for examination. They 'have to use their own common sense, and if they do not their action will be to their own disadvantage. Were it possible to have periodical examinations certain diseases w-ould be discovered through diagnosis.
I have mentioned certain diseases in connection with which great improvement has been shorvn. There are others, however, in which the figures are not so encouraging. In 1926 there were 7.C14 deaths from cancer whereas in 1933 there were 10.646. Cancer is one disease which if situated in certain parts of the body could be discovered by means of periodical health examinations. Particularly is that true of external cancers, wdiere cures 92582-12^
could be effected if treatment were begun earlier. It is largely due to the fact that the disease is not found early enough that the death rate is gradually mounting higher and higher. In the year 1926 there were 11.415 deaths from heart disease, whereas in 1933 there were 15.483. These figures show a very great increase. Heart disease is another ailment which could be discovered in its early state and treatment or suggestions as to mode of life given which would be found very beneficial. Last summer in nearly every paper one read he would find an account of some well known person who had dropped dead on a golf course, or on the street or at home. Some of those men were in the prime of life, between the ages of forty-five and fifty. Undoubtedly these ailments had developed insidiously but could have been discovered had there been periodical health examinations. I cannot urge too strongly my approval of the hon. member's observations concerning the necessity for such examinations.
Despite all the advances in the science of medicine and despite the splendid service medical practice can give, the difficulty is to make those advances available to the great masses of the people. I believe that is the gist of the hon. member's resolution; undoubtedly he would like to see measures taken to make the results of modern medical science available to every one. That brings before us the question of state medicine. As there are some who entertain doubts as to the meaning of that term, perhaps I might read what the Canadian Medical Association believes to be the purpose of state medicine. I quote from a report made by a committee of doctors:
The ultimate purpose of any plan is to make available for every Canadian the full benefits of curative and preventive medicine, irrespective of individual ability to pay, and, at the same time, to assure the practitioners of medicine and others associated in the provision of medical care a reasonable remuneration for their services.
The purpose first stated in this quotation is, I think, what we are all aiming at, namely to make the full benefits of curative and preventive medicine available to all. But in any move of the kind which a government, either federal or provincial, might make, it is essential to consider the matter and discuss it with the medical associations, because on their cooperation the success of the whole thing depends. The Canadian Medical Association, realizing that this subject was becoming a very important one to the provinces, to the dominion and to all our citizens,



Health Policy-Mr. Sutherland
appointed not long ago a committee to go thoroughly into the matter. The committee has made a comprehensive report considering the subject, I think, from every angle, and the present situation is this:	The Canadian
Medical Association has sent that plan to each provincial body, and the provincial bodies in turn have sent it to every individual doctor throughout the country for his observations and any suggestions he desires to make upon it. The comments and suggestions which the individual doctors make will come back through the provincial bodies to the Canadian Medical Association and from their replies and the original plan it will be possible for the association to evolve some plan which they can recommend to some government. It does seem to me that until that plan is evolved and ready to be presented to a government, steps should not be taken in the matter, because there is no use going into a thing of this kind at random and without seeing just where you are going. Of course it is the desire of all governments to get all the information they can along these lines.
One part of the motion which the hon. member for Battle River has presented has to do with cooperation between the dominion and the provinces. We have cooperation at present along those lines. That is the policy of the federal Department of Health, to cooperate in every way with the provinces. We have at the present time the Dominion Council of Health which consists of the chief medical officer of health for each of the .provinces, together with a representative of labour, a representative of agriculture, a representative of the urban and rural women's organizations, one scientific adviser, and the deputy minister of the Department of Pensions and National Health. The council is brought to Ottawa twice a year at the expense of the dominion government, when they go thoroughly into the various problems that each has met with in his own part of the country. One of those meetings has been held since I came to this department, and I know 'that it was very beneficial. Some of the representatives of the provinces who were present have written that they considered the meeting this year of great benefit to them and to the people of their provinces. That activity will be continued, of course, and we expect great benefits to come from it.
But there is another step which I intend to take. It is my purpose to invite at some mutually convenient time within the next two or three months the ministers of health of the various provinces to come to Ottawa and discuss with me their problems, with the
[Mr. Sutherland.!
idea, just as the hon. member for Battle River suggests, of furthering cooperation between the federal and provincial bodies, because I am firmly convinced that any advances that are to be made will be made only along the lines of that cooperation. In extending that invitation to the provincial ministers of health I am in hopes that much good will come of our meeting.
I have endeavoured, Mr. Speaker, to give a general summary of the position in regard to public health in Canada at the present time. I have no objection to this motion passing because I am quite in sympathy with it. Our policy at the present time is cooperation and anything that I can do to further that policy I shall be only too glad to do during the time I hold this office.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	Mr. Speaker, I have been very much
interested in the speeches made by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) and the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Sutherland). The hon. member for Battle River deserves a great deal of credit for bringing before the House of Commons year after year this matter of a national health program.
Lest I forget it may I say at once that I do not agree with the statement made by the minister that the Canadian Medical Association should be the one to evolve a health policy, or that the federal government should make no move until the medical association had decided what should be done. I do not think that is so at all. In the first place, doctors are trained at very great expense to the provinces, because the universities are certainly not self-sustaining. In a measure doctors are public servants; they have shown that magnificently during these trying four years. I am sure they can offer valuable suggestions, but I do not for a moment think that the federal government should wait for the pronouncement of the medical association. The federal government itself should evolve a health policy, whether it be one with many branches, such as health insurance and county health units, or whatever it may be. The federal government, I say, should do the evolving, perhaps with the cooperation of the provinces and the Canadian Medical Association.
In my opinion the main reason why medical science is not available to all the people is the lack of money on the part of the people. I notice in this little pamphlet which the Canadian Social Hygiene Council has sent to us, entitled Canada at War, the statement is

Health Policy-Miss Macphail
made that public health officials agree that sickness costs the people of Canada over $311,000,000 a year, and that almost nine-tenths of this represents a direct charge upon the individual. Well, I think the direct charge upon the individual is greater than the individual can bear, and people are going without the benefits of medical science simply because they cannot afford to pay for it. It causes the death of many of them, which I suppose is just as much expense, but the particular individual affected does not need to worry about that expense.
In confirmation of that, I notice that in an article in the Canadian Home Journal of May, 1934, Norma Phillips Muir makes this statement with reference to maternal mortality :
One doctor whose professional life has been pretty well given to studying public health and preventive medicine has stated that actually there is no maternal mortality problem in Canada-that it is a problem of dollars and cents because the deaths can to a very great extent be prevented if the pregnant woman and medical and nursing services are brought together.
I think what is true in regard to maternal mortality is true also of many diseases. The very rich can afford to have care for the prevention and cure of disease whenever they desire. It is also true that the very poor in cities like Toronto, as mentioned by the Minister of Health, are given very, good care indeed. But there is a large middle class between the rich and the poor who actually cannot afford to have good care when sickness comes. I know there are splendid hospitals and doctors and nurses, but what does that matter when the people cannot get into the hospital without guaranteeing payment, and when they have not the money to pay for care in the hospitals? In the city of Owen Sound people have actually been kept waiting on the steps of the hospital until the hospital authorities could be assured there was going to be full pay for their hospitalization. Everyone in this house knows of innumerable instances where people have not been able to secure hospital treatment or the care of a nurse in their own home simply because they could not afford to pay for it. There are hundreds and thousands of nurses out of work in Canada who would be only too glad to take care of the sick, as the sick would be only too glad to be taken care of. But there must be dollars to bridge the chasm between unemployed nurses and uncared for sick.
I was very glad to notice that Ontario has this year established its first health unit,
as reported in the Ottawa Journal of Thursday, December 13. That unit will cover the counties of Stormont, Glengarry, Prescott and Russell. The Rockefeller foundation is making a grant of $33,000 and the unit will employ five nurses. The administrative officer and his nursing staff of five will conduct health administration, education, sanitation, public health nursing and the control of communicable diseases. At present 2,000 children in the four municipalities have received dental attention and one hundred per cent have received immunization from diphtheria. After the three year period the grant of $33,000 ceases and the cost must be borne by the counties and the provincial authorities.
I am particularly concerned about having county health units in all counties because they can do a great deal to prevent disease and I think it is better both from the point of view of human happiness and from the economic standpoint. In the long run it costs less and certainly people are much happier when well. In my opinion a great deal can be done by preventive medicine. Perhaps I might take a moment to say what has been done in Owen Sound particularly, through the work of Doctor Murray, who has devoted his attention to prevention. He has made a particular study of preventive medicine. In Owen Sound they now have free clinics for the early diagnosis of tuberculosis and for venereal disease. They have a free child clinic and last year they had a free dental clinic for school children. It is interesting to know that two or three years ago the death rate in Owen Sound among children under one year of age was the lowest in Ontario and the second in Canada, being excelled by Victoria, British Columbia.
Everyone interested in this matter feels that other municipalities could obtain similar results if they followed similar methods. I should like very much to have a county health unit in Grey county, for this reason particularly, that that county is as beset with contagious diseases and other ills as any other county and suffers in addition the disability of goitre to a greater extent than in any other county. I said once in public that fifty per cent of the people in Grey county suffered from goitre in some form and I was laughed to scorn. Well, Doctor Murray of Owen Sound and Doctor Carefoot of Markdale made a careful analysis, each over a certain area, and they found that it went well over fifty per cent; they said that the figure I gave was too low. And yet that terrific responsibility must be carried by the people

Health Policy-Mr. Morand
of Grey county. It is entirely unfair and, what is more, they are not able to do it. From my own personal experience this year among my own friends I know of at least ten people in the late fifties who no doubt died of goitre. Possibly on the death certificate goitre would not be given as the cause of death, but the doctors attending them assured me that it was, having resulted in a heart condition which was the actual cause of death, or in an anaemic condition, or in some other of the complications that ensue. Unless you attend a great many meetings, picnics and one thing and another and see people in large numbers you will not believe how prevalent it is. I do feel that it is not fair to ask the individual to pay for the treatment of a disease which is caused by deficiency in the soil of the district. If we are to have health units in any part of Ontario it is not unreasonable to urge that Grey county and possibly Bruce as well should be the district in which experimentation is carried on.
I have asked the federal Department of Health as well as the provincial government to make a survey of the county to see whether or not goitre is as terrible there as we who live in the county think it is, but in both cases an investigation of any sort has been refused. If the governments in Canada are not going to take the responsibility who is to assume it? One would be almost humiliated to go to New York and ask the Rockefeller people to make the survey, because surely it is a responsibility that lies within this country. In supporting this general resolution asking that the federal government adopt a definite health policy to be carried out in cooperation with the provincial governments I am not thinking only of this one particular area, but I am thinking of it especially because the need is so great.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ADOPTION OP POLICY IN COOPERATION WITH THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
It is with a great deal of pleasure that I congratulate the mover of this motion (Mr. Spencer) on the humanitarian stand he has taken and on the very interesting and definite method he proposes of correlating the work of medicine in Canada.
Medicine has made rapid strides when one looks back over history and realizes that it has grown to a very comprehensive science from early beginnings of empiricism and a great deal of superstition. It has been certainly an individual science, and its advance has been entirely an individual matter. It is an individual type of occupation and consequently the organization of medicine has

probably not advanced or kept step with the organization of other fields of activity.
On could very well divide the value of medicine into two distinct and different fields. First of all there is the preventive and then the curative. Then again one could divide preventive medicine into two distinct subdivisions, that which applies particularly to the public or to the state and the community, such as the control of contagious diseases and the control of those diseases that come under the supervision of public health officials, and then the preventive measures which are entirely individual, in relation to those diseases that are not communicable but if taken in hand early may be prevented from the natural consequences which follow unless proper treatment is given.
In the first division, diseases that are communicable and generally within the community, most of the necessity is not so much within the field of medicine as it is within that of education. It is education that is needed to teach the people the value of preventives now at hand. Education is necessary to teach them how to prevent some very simple conditions and I was very much interested in listening to the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) when she spoke of thyroid in her particular county. It seems to me that that trouble, its cause and prevention, are now so generally known and the prevention is so simple, that I am amazed that within that county the authorities now in charge have not seen fit to advise or educate their people in the very simple matter of taking of a few drops of iodine once or twice a month, which would entirely prevent the condition which now exists. I shall not attempt to enumerate all the very many good works that have already been accomplished by preventive means, such as the control of typhoid, scarlet fever, diphtheria, whooping cough and other communicable diseases which to-day have almost disappeared and would be still further controlled as a result of a simple and general education among the people.
The part of preventive medicine from which it seems to be the most difficult to secure the maximum benefit is that which applies to the individual himself. The minister a few minutes ago spoke about heart diseases and other conditions. Those are conditions which are essentially individual and the question is not one of cost; it is a question not of necessity but of driving home to the people the importance of constant supervision by their medical men. On the other hand, the part that interests me most is the securing of the maximum benefit that is available within the

Health Policy-Mr. Mitchell
science of medicine to those who are unable to pay for it. Strange as it may seem, it is not the poorest who are unable to pay; it is that large class of people between those on relief, those in abject poverty, and the very rich. Medicine has evolved from the simple application of one man's view, one man's ability, one man's science. To-day we have available in the various sciences-electricity, mathematics, medicine, and so forth-large laboratories and expensive equipment, and in the field of medical science these developments have increased the cost of medicine, the cost of treatment and cure and, more particularly, the cost of diagnosis, beyond the ability to pay of the average man who is trying to carry on for himself.
As regards those who are poor, I was astounded to learn that in some hospitals they are permitted to stand on the steps because they cannot pay. In twenty years' rather active practice I have yet to find a hospital refuse to take a patient because he could not pay. But there is a large class of people who, because of small salaries, because they are anxious to pay their way, find it impossible or are very reluctant to spend the necessary money to secure the diagonsis and the maximum that science has to give. X-ray is very expensive; laboratory tests are expensive; heart treatment and heart diagnosis instruments are to-day quite expensive. Day after day people come into our offices where the aid of these branches of science is necessary to make a complete diagnosis and to give them the maximum that is available within the science of medicine. These people cannot or feel they should not spend the amount necessary to secure the benefit of the science, consequently the maximum benefits of the science are available only to those who are very poor, whom the state now takes care of, or to those who are wealthy and to whom cost makes no difference. But the very large mass of the people, probably the most important class in the community, find themselves only too often unable to secure the maximum benefit that they should receive. This is rather discouraging to a medical man who from day to day has in his office patients who are unable to secure the full benefit that science can offer. Organization in medicine is undoubtedly necessary at this time. Organization has taken place in every other field of activity, but medicine continues very much in its individual application of the best that each medical man has to offer. Some day within the not very far distant future I hope to see some scheme evolved for that class of people who, too often optimistic in the belief that
physical ills will not affect them, and probably because of low salaries or wages unable to set anything aside, find themselves confronted when they least expect it with large bills, perhaps at a time when the head of the house has no earning capacity. I hope to see a scheme put into operation whereby men in receipt of earnings under a certain amount per annum may pool a part of their earnings in order to create a fund, with the aid of the state and the employer, to enable them to secure the maximum that medical science has to offer them. Further, I would like to see them secure aid when they are ill so that they may feel a sense of security during that most trying of times, a security which comes from the knowledge that if they wish to take advantage of it they can avail themselves of what is in store for them within the field of medical science.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ADOPTION OP POLICY IN COOPERATION WITH THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had some experience in this matter, having been a member of the hospital board in my own municipality for the past ten years, and also a member of the board of health for many years. This question is being very actively discussed throughout the North American continent.
I was amused by the observation made by the minister that it would be necessary to consult the doctors before any scheme of this description could be launched. If I remember rightly, when Mr. Lloyd George introduced his health insurance scheme in Great Britain, the greatest opposition came from the doctors. Those who have traced the history of its development will well remember the indignation meetings held by the doctors of Great Britain in opposition to the scheme; yet to-day the selfsame people who opposed it so violently are those who admit its soundness and its practicability in that great country. In fact, thev have gone so far that in the last three months I understand the medical men of Great Britain have affiliated with the British Trades Union Congress. I hope we shall live to see the day when such a departure is made in this dominion.
Quite recently in the United States they appointed a committee on costs of medical care, which was aided by finances supplied by the Rockefeller or the Carnegie foundation. That committee, composed of representatives of the doctors, of labour, of the teaching profession and others sat for five years and brought in a report in which they eulogized the experiment being made in Saskatchewan in connection with what I suppose may be

Health Policy-Mr. Mitchell
called socialized medicine. In their third recommendation they say:
The committee recommends that the costs of medical care be placed on a group payment basis, through the use of insurance, through the use of taxation, or through the use of both these methods. This is not meant to preclude the continuation of medical service provided on an individual fee basis for those who prefer the present method. Cash benefits, i.e. compensation for wage loss due to illness, if and when provided, should be separate and distinct from medical services.
So we can see how in the country to the south they are progressing towards a policy of collectivization in the treatment of the sick.
Two years ago a commission appointed by the government of British Columbia recommended a scheme of health insurance in that province. And we have this committee of the Canadian Medical Association, spoken of by the minister this evening, which is giving leadership to the various medical societies throughout the dominion. This is all in line with a recognition of the responsibility of the community as such for the treatment of the sick. In connection with preventive medicine the state has gone into the field in the matter of insane, and venereal disease, diphtheria, tuberculosis and many other diseases have been practically taken out of the hands of the general medical profession and their treatment placed upon a state basis.
One of the greatest problems at the moment, particularly in connection with this depression, is seen for instance in a city like Toronto where the medical needs of 26,000 families are being cared for by the municipality. It is unfair to expect the general practitioner to render his services on the basis that prevails at present in many localities, that is, free of charge, although I know that in accordance with the traditions of the profession it has been customary for him to give those very necessary services wherever they were required by those unable to pay. What the hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Mo-rand) said this evening is quite true. In my community I know of no instance where any individual has been denied treatment in any of our hospitals through lack of financial resources, whether it be the municipal hospital or St. Joseph's, which is of course a sectarian hospital. I think it is a fair observation to make that the indigent patient in the hospitals of this country receives treatment on a par with the wealthiest, because we insist that the surgeons on the staffs of civic hospitals shall be at the top of their profession in their respective districts. These indigent mt.ients do not have to take the IMr. Mitchell.J
chance, like the great middle class, of getting, maj? I gay, an inferior grade of practitioner. The municipality I come from insists that the best in surgery shall be given to those unable to pay. Nor is it fair and equitable that those who are able to pay should have placed upon them the burden of the care of the indigent. At present they have to bear the expense in a broad way of those unable to pay. Some policy should be worked out whereby the expense is placed broadly on the whole community, and I know of no better system than that set up in (Great Britain and in other countries in Europe to deal with the problem.
It seems to me also that having regard to the work being done in our hospital centres, particularly during this depression, the personal touch of the family physician is more or less lost. Under a system of health insurance there would be a movement back to the family physician. The present practice is too mechanized. There is no substitute in the field of medicine for the understanding and care that can come about only through the long continued association of the family physician with his people.
_ As a matter of equity the medical profession should not be asked to render the enormous services they are being asked to render to-day absolutely free of charge. I have often said that medicine stands to-day in the same relationship to the community as schools did a century ago. In those days in regard to education you paid for what you got. In the evolution of our civilization and the desire of our people for a general educational system the responsibility for education was taken over by the state. I believe that is an inevitable development in regard to medical service in its broadest aspect. I do not mean that everyone should be covered by an insurance system. I think the hon. member for East Essex expressed the idea correctly when he said that that great group in between should have facilities placed at their disposal whereby the tremendous expense involved by ill health should be borne in a cooperative way. I suppose we all know of many families in which a major illness has been a financial tragedy, and any policy that the government or the medical profession can set up that will eliminate the fear of that condition from the lives of that great body of people who like to pay for the services they receive would be a distinct advance. I do not believe that any nation can be built on "something for nothing." A sense of obligation to meet their financial responsibilities has been one of the great driving forces in the development of this nation.

Health Policy-Mr. Sproule
I was glad to hear the minister make the observations he did, that the federal government in connection with the provincial governments and these agencies of public opinion, in combination with the medical profession, should study this question deeply. They can rest assured that the labour forces of the dominion will lend their sympathetic aid to the formulation of a policy not only in the interests of the people but also in the best interest of the medical profession itself, which in the past, and particularly during this depression, has rendered such fine service to the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take any part in this discussion, but after listening to my friend the hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Morand) and the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) I wish to say a few words. Some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) touch closely the situation in my own section. I think the hon. member for East Essex was correct when he said that it was not the poorest class nor the richest class that was neglected; there is the in-between class who feel themselves hardly able to pay the doctors' bills. I believe in many cases they neglect their health simply because they remember the last doctor's bill they received, and they remember having to sell the last cow, the last pig or something else in order to get the money with which to pay it. They feel, and rightly, that they should keep the doctor paid up, because they do not know how soon they may need his aid again.
I have a great deal of sympathy for the medical men; I understand that some of them in Toronto last year, after spending a great deal of time and money on their education, had to go on relief. I hope that was not true, but I remember having heard it. On the other hand I know that in the rural district from which I come they bitterly complain that the bills in many cases are too high. The charge now is $5 a call, where possibly when that man was young the charge was only 81 or $2 for the same trip. The farmer did not mind so much when he could sell a bushel of wheat for a dollar and a cow or horse for $100; he walked to the telephone and called the doctor without hesitation. Unfortunately to-day most of the farmers do not have telephones. At one time they were considered necessities, but now they are considered more in the way of luxuries. Perhaps that is something else that might be looked into; to-day the cost of a telephone is the same as it 'was in the palmy days.
There is no doubt that the poorer class can get medical assistance quite easily, because the health officer or medical board has authority to act, but that is not the case in regard to the man in between, who is not in a position to ask for assistance or who does not feel like asking for it. As a result he neglects the trouble for a day or two too long. The poor people who have been on relief call up the reeve of the municipality, and he realizes that he must take care of them. The other man, however, is not so fortunate; the reeve has to call a council meeting to find out whether or not he has authority to act, and then the chances are that the council will decide that the man can sell another cow or pig and pay the doctor, so they take no action. So I think the sooner something is done along the lines set out in this resolution the better it will be for all concerned.
Just here I would like to say a word about the poor children who are not properly clothed to go to school. Their clothing is not sufficient; their shoes are thin, and in rainy weather their feet must be wet when they get to school. Most of the school teachers take wonderful care of the children, providing them with hot lunches, and so on, but they should not 'be required to do that.
I was very much amused at some of the discussion in connection with the building scheme that was under consideration this evening. When you really consider it, many of the cities are not nearly so badly off as the small rural communities are. I think perhaps the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) put the -matter rather well when she said that while many of the homes looked bad enough from the road, they look worse when you get inside. Hon. members who come from rural districts and who are acquainted with these conditions will agree when I say that, while the health officer perhaps should go to these homes and see that they are kept in a healthier condition, that health officer, in order to do so, would have to pass many other homes of the same class, and it is hardly worth his while. It is too bad the houses and outbuildings have fallen into such disrepair, and it is too bad that something cannot be done about it.
There has been a great deal of agitation in connection with the construction of public buildings, but I can say that the agriculturists at present are more in need of relief than any other class. If they have their health they can put up with a great deal, and I hope something can be done along the line of this resolution. As a rule very little public money is spent in the rural districts; generally it goes to the larger centres, which have better
Health Policy-Mr. Sproule

representation in this house. Rural constituencies cover large areas; most of them do not need wharves or large hotels or anything of that kind, and the result is that when the estimates are brought down they contain nothing for the rural constituencies. You look in the blue book to see how much is going to be spent in your district, but you cannot find the name of the place from which you come, so you know that no public money will be spent there. Then when you look around to see where the money is to be spent you find that large amounts are to go to the more thickly populated districts. In most of the rural districts when they speak of money they speak of hundreds of thousands of dollars, but when we come here we speak about millions of dollars. I can say frankly that the man on the back concession does not understand language of that kind; he does not know what it means. If you tell him that he could not live long enough to count it all, after he considers that statement for some time he begins to realize just what it means. Many times I have thought about some of these hotels that have been built here and there, costing millions of dollars, That money would go a long way in preserving the lives of our poor children who are so badly neglected. The chances are that when that hotel is built it will lose a quarter of a million dollars or so a year, and even that amount would do a great deal of good if it were devoted to the welfare of the children. I do say it is very hard to get anything in a rural constituency, and it is hard to tell a man who comes from the city how much in need the people are on these back concessions.
I remember the occasion when I attended the good roads convention in Toronto. I have been a director of the good roads association for some time, and this year I happen to be president. When elected president one of the directors came to me and said, " You ire the man who came in here twelve or fifteen years ago and began talking about growing beets and, because of the mud, having to draw them out a quarter of a ton at a time. Have you those mud roads down there yet?" I replied, " They have been very much improved "-and that is a fact. In good times it was easy to get improvements, but when prices dropped and times were not so good we found it more difficult to get improvements. I realize that we are living in one of the most fortunate countries in the world; we are making a speedy recovery, but I do think it is up to the people to realize what those on the back concessions require. It is very difficult to impress mem-
bers of the House of Commons with what their requirements are, because the average member is not aware of them.
Although the hon. member for Southeast Grey and I do not agree on many questions I will say that she and some other hon. members in that corner of the house have tried on many occasions to stress the needs of the back concessions, and sometimes we have found it difficult to make our wants known. I do not think most people realize how much improvements are needed. It is the duty of the man who comes from the rural district to try to fight his battle as best he can, and if we do not get results as soon as we would like we may get a better footing a little later on.
I am in agreement with other hon. members who have stated that health is a most necessary factor in the enjoyment' of life, and I do hope that the present resolution is not dropped. I must say however that I cannot altogether agree with some observations of medical men. In my view the reeves of some municipalities could tell more about actual requirements than some medical men. I do not suppose many medical men will agree with me when I make the statement I am about to make, but I believe I am showing all due respect and am fair to that profession when I observe that there should be some way of knowing what a medical man will charge when he is called. When a person on a back concession calls a doctor he is wondering all the time how much he will be charged. He may be in such doubt that he will delay telephoning or sending word because he wonders if he will ever be able to pay his doctor's bill. It seems to me there ought to be some way of knowing. When we call a taxi we have some idea what the charge will be. Turning again to professional men, we have a good idea what a lawyer will charge us and if we are not satisfied we are free to tax his bill.

I am quite content to listen to the information and am very pleased to get it. Some people have had the experience of calling medical men in our section of the country and have been surprised when they have received their bills. I know of one man who asked his medical man for an itemized bill and received a reply to this effect: "The itemized bill will be $15 more because you did not pay it yesterday." I am wondering if there is any possible way of being certain what we must pay. In my constituency I know of a case where a poor lad ran into an electric wire and was badly burned. Hon. members know that the municipalities carry insurance. As a result of his burns some insurance was coming to him, but when his doctor's bill was received he found he had a very little left. The case was taken to court and the judge reduced the fee by S200, but I think if another $200 had been deducted the doctor would still have been paid too much. However, I am very pleased to receive the information from the hon. member and shall be happy to take it back to my friends.
As the representative of the constituency of East Lambton I am going to try to bring the grievances of my constituents before this chamber and make an effort to have some of them ironed out. I do not know how you can check up on a doctor's bill. He may make a dozen calls on a trip, and possibly he may charge $2 for each call. I am not stating the doctors are dishonest; as a matter of fact I believe they are honest, but-
